News.title: ‘Taxi driver’, 45, is arrested over ‘spying for Iran’ at RAF base in Cyprus targeted by barrage of drones
News.content:
'SPY' ARREST ‘Taxi driver’, 45, is arrested over ‘spying for Iran’ at RAF base in Cyprus targeted by barrage of drones

A BRITISH “taxi driver” has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Iran at an RAF base in Cyprus – which was later targeted by drones.

Rashad Sultanov, 44 – a dual UK and Azerbaijani national – is accused of sharing information with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).



Sultanov was arrested on July 17 by Cypriot authorities and is currently being held in custody as extradition proceedings remain ongoing.

His arrest comes after counter-terror cops investigated incidents at RAF Akrotiri between May 11 and June 11 last year.



Just months later, the UK’s key Mediterranean base was blitzed by Iranian suicide drones, with a naval warship later sent to defend the island.

Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) officials have since authorised charges against Sultanov under section 3 and 4 of the National Security Act.



Commander Helen Flanagan said: “This case shows we are able to use the National Security Act overseas when British military bases are allegedly targeted by hostile state activity.

“A huge amount of partnership work has been carried out between British and Cypriot law enforcement agencies.

“We continue to work with colleagues from the CPS, National Crime Agency and Cypriot authorities as extradition proceedings progress.”

Britain retains two sovereign base areas in Cyprus, RAF Akrotiri and Dhekelia, under a treaty agreed upon independence in 1960.



They are used to support British military operations in the Middle East.

Cyprus’ President Nikos Christodoulides later demanded negotiations over the bases.

The RAF Akrotiri strike and subsequent delays in deploying a Royal Navy warship to the region have strained relations.

Christodoulides said there must be an “open and frank discussion” with the UK about the bases, which he described as a “colonial consequence”.

He told reporters: “When this situation is over in the Middle East, we are going to have an open and frank discussion with the British Government.”



Earlier this month, the Home Office confirmed support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps would be banned for the first time.

Sweeping new national security powers made it a crime to support or assist the group.

Anyone found backing the IRGC could face up to 14 years behind bars.

And those carrying out espionage, sabotage or foreign interference on its behalf could face life in prison.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The move follows a series of arson attacks and intimidation campaigns targeting Jewish communities and Israeli interests in Britain.



The IRGC has long been accused of plotting intimidation, kidnappings and assassination attempts abroad, including threats to people in the UK.

News.title: ‘Black Widow’ carer arrested at airport as she returns to UK to be jailed after she kept OAP like ‘animal’ & stole £300k
News.content:
FINALLY CAGED ‘Black Widow’ carer arrested at airport as she returns to UK to be jailed after she kept OAP like ‘animal’ & stole £300k

A FRAUDSTER dubbed “the Black Widow” has finally been arrested after she returned to the UK to face justice for her crimes.

Pamela Gwinnett, 63, stole £300,000 from her “cash cow” Joan Greene and fled the country before she could be brought to justice.



She absconded to Tenerife and for the last year has been sunbathing and relaxing at her holiday home, The Sun revealed.

Greater Manchester Police worked with the National Crime Agency to track down Gwinnett and start the legal process of bringing her back to the UK.



Pictures show the 62-year-old being escorted by GMP officers from the Terminal 3 arrival lounge at Manchester Airport into a police van.

Gwinnett was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison in her absence in October 2025 for a variety of offences including fraud by abuse of position and theft.

Originally from Adlington, Cheshire, the fraudster systematically plundered thousands from retired accountant Joan after setting herself up as the pensioner’s carer.

Gwinnett then spent money she stole from the “frail” 89-year-old on an Audi Q2, expensive meals, designer clothes, mortgages and Botox.



The carer seemingly hid her evil intentions behind a friendly façade, all the while keeping the vulnerable OAP caged like an animal at her home in Chorley.

To maintain control over her “cash cow,” Gwinnett isolated Joan from her family, convincing the pensioner that her own relatives were stealing from her.

Tragically, Joan died in 2022 after spending her final years being “bullied” by the woman who was supposed to be caring for her.

But her neighbours had no idea.

She continued to steal money from Joan, 89, even after the pensioner passed away.



The carer was then arrested for fraud by abuse of position and theft but released on bail.

She then applied for permission to fly to Tenerife, claiming she needed to scatter her brother’s ashes, which the court refused.

But five hours later, she was on a plane and fled the UK.

The Sun previously revealed the fugitive was hiding in plain sight, flaunting her freedom by sunbathing and going to bars in Tenerife.

She was living in a penthouse apartment in a sunny town on the south-west coast of Tenerife, according to locals. It has since been locked up and the outside furniture taken in.



It is understood she also owns another apartment, which The Sun found on various holiday let websites priced at £112 a night.

The lavish seaside property has access to a pool, “stunning views”, a balcony, a big TV and a more than 8 out of 10 rating on a booking website.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She will appear at Preston Crown Court later today relating to her previous failure to appear at court.

News.title: Fire crews battle through night as Suffolk wildfire spreads to ‘210 football pitches’ after terrified families evacuated
News.content:
FIRE crews have been battling through the night to tackle the raging Suffolk wildfire – which has spread to the size of 210 football pitches.

Some 120 firefighters have been dousing the devastating inferno, as shell-shocked families were evacuated from their homes near Dunwich Heath.



The “large-scale, wind-driven” blaze – which broke out at 5.30pm on Wednesday – was declared a major incident the following morning.

Dozens of nearby homes and holiday parks were among those evacuated as the fire devoured the tinder-dry grassland.



Smoke could be seen billowing into the sky for miles around, with nearby nuclear station Sizewell B put on “high alert”.

Fire chiefs now say the scale of the raging blaze stretches a whopping 150 hectares – the equivalent of approximately 210 football pitches.

Alex Drew told The Sun how he was woken by his terrified daughter Ayla, eight, at 3am on Thursday as the blaze threatened their caravan.

He said: “We’d been out for the day and arrived back at around 5.20pm.



“We saw some people looking out over a field and thought they’d maybe seen a deer or something.

“But then we saw a little bit of smoke and realised there was a fire.

“There was a woman on the phone to the emergency services and then we saw two fire engines race by.”

But Alex said he “didn’t think much of it” and the pair both went to bed, before they were awoken to cops banging on their caravan door.

“The next thing I knew, Ayla was waking me up,” Alex continued.



“She’d been woken by the police banging on the door telling us we needed to leave immediately.

“She was terrified, as you can imagine. We packed up and got out straight away.

“I told the police I’d had two beers, so they breathalysed me and said I was fine to jump in the car.



“It was 3am, so we just drove down to the beach and watched the sunrise.”

The fire service said its response to the fire would continue for another 48 hours at least.

Changing wind conditions are making it difficult to predict how it may spread, the service added.

On Thursday evening, Suffolk’s chief fire officer, Jon Lacey, confirmed 120 firefighters were involved in the response.

He said: “Eighteen fire engines and 120 firefighters are involved in the response.



“But difficult terrain and limited access routes are making it hard for crews to reach some areas of the wildfire.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He confirmed approximately 100 to 150 people had been evacuated from their accommodation.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham vowed to send “all the support” necessary.

News.title: Hamas agrees to ‘complete disarmament’ in Gaza as Trump hails ‘historic’ step towards peace hopes in Middle East
News.content:
DONALD Trump’s Board of Peace has reached a crucial agreement with Hamas for the “complete disarmament” of the terror group in Gaza.

The “historic breakthrough” saw Hamas agree to lay down its weapons with Israel now set to completely withdraw from Gaza after over 1,000 days of fighting.



The militant group’s disarmament was one of the main issues during truce talks since a fragile ceasefire was implemented last October.

US President Donald Trump made the announcement on Truth Social overnight as he said the deal also applies to all armed groups in Gaza.



Hamas’ terror tunnels and infrastructure built since the October 7 massacre in 2023 will also be dismantled.

He added: “The agreement will be carried out in carefully structured phases.”

This includes the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the establishing of a new Palestinian government.

Hamas officials said a committee established by the Board of Peace will help govern Gaza and oversee the process of storing the weapons.

Trump went on to say: “One year ago there was a violent raging war, humanitarian crisis and hostages kept in brutal captivity.

“We have made historic progress and there is still much work to do.



“Congratulations to all on this amazing development that everybody daif could never be achieved.”

The Board of Peace brokered the deal alongside allies from Turkey, Egypt, Qatar and the United States.

They said they got Hamas to agree to a “detailed roadmap”.



A statement added: “The agreement concludes months of intensive, good faith negotiations to advance President Donald J. Trump’s vision for establishing new governance, security, humanitarian relief, reconstruction, and economic recovery in Gaza.

“The roadmap represents a historic breakthrough.

“For the first time, Hamas officially has committed to an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons, which will be followed by Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.”

A Board of Peace spokesperson said the hard work is only partially done as their attention now turns to implementing the deal.

Ghazi Hamad, a member of Hamas’ negotiating team, said they have made “concessions for the sake of our people in the Gaza Strip”.



“The agreement contains a clear provision stating that Israel must commit to and implement its obligations. If Israel does not implement the agreement, neither will we,” Hamad added.

Israel are yet to respond to news of the agreement.

What happened on October 7? ON October 7 2023, militants of Hamas and other Palestinian nationalist groups launched co-ordinated armed attacks in the Gaza Envelope of southern Israel. The perpetrators had managed to bypass Israeli defences to para-glide across the border, in what became the first invasion of the territory since the 1948 Arab-Israeli War. The horror coincided with the Jewish celebration of Simchat Torah, and initiated the ongoing Israel-Hamas War. A barrage of around 4,300 rockets were launched on Israel from the Gaza Strip in the early hours of October 7 before vehicles and powered paragliders crossed the border. Hamas fighters attacked military bases and massacred civilians in 21 communities, including Be’eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz, Netiv Haasara, and Alumim. The first civilian attack started at 6.29am at the Nova Music Festival site at Re’im, just three miles from Gaza. More than 360 revellers were cut down as they desperately tried to flee. Across October 7, an estimated 1,139 people were massacred and another 251 civilians and soldiers were taken hostage into Gaza.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did hold talks with Trump in Washington earlier this week.

The war in Gaza started over 1,000 days ago after Hamas gunmen stormed the Nova Festival and killed 1,195 people including a 14-hour-old baby and 18 British nationals.



Around 251 people were taken hostage and forced to live in captivity – some for over 500 days.

In response, Israel launched a deadly war which claimed the lives of ten of thousands of Hamas operatives and Palestinian civilians.

Israel launched near daily strikes for almost two years as Netanyahu vowed to kill every last Hamas member to completely eradicate the group.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Trump quickly got involved as he returned to the White House in January 2025 as he helped broker a peace deal which took effect on October 10.

Israeli strikes have drastically lessened since the war in Iran plunged the Middle East into further chaos.

News.title: Woman sexually assaulted at town centre bus station in early hours attack as cops release CCTV in hunt for man
News.content:
ATTACK PROBE Woman sexually assaulted at town centre bus station in early hours attack as cops release CCTV in hunt for man

AN INVESTIGATION has been launched after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted at a bus station in the early hours.

Cops have released CCTV in the urgent hunt for a man after the horror reportedly unfolded in Wigan, Greater Manchester, last Sunday.



The victim is said to have been targeted at the town centre bus station at around 4.15am.

Police patrols have since been stepped up at the station and across the town, Greater Manchester Police said.



The force has since released an urgent appeal for information following the attack, which is believed to be “isolated”.

CCTV footage of a man cops wish to speak to in connection with the alleged assault has since been shared across social media.



Inspector Lisa Morris said: “We have launched an investigation into this incident and are making a number of enquiries at pace to locate the person responsible.

“We are appealing to anyone who was in the area at the time or may recognise this individual as we believe he may be able to help with our investigation.

“Anyone with information, or anyone who knows the man pictured are asked to contact the Wigan Neighbourhood Team on 0161 856 7160 quoting log 505 of 26.07.26.

“Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.



“We believe this to be an isolated incident, but in order to reassure the public and those visiting or living in the town centre, patrols have been increased in the area.”

News.title: Jewel thieves jailed for 15 years after nicking £225,000 of gems in smash & grab with sledgehammer
News.content:
THREE balaclava-clad thugs who carried out a brazen daylight smash-and-grab at a family jeweller and stole £225,000 worth of gems have been caged.

Trio Deniz Mehmet, 28, Lee Ramsey, 46, and Robert Clarke, 50, targeted Gregory & Co jewellers in Richmond, south west London, on January 31.



They admitted conspiracy to rob and were each sentenced for five years and three months at Kingston Crown Court yesterday (July 30).

The combined sentences total 15 years and nine months behind bars.



Shocking footage of the raid – which later went viral – showed the gang relentlessly battering their way into the family-run shop.

Witnesses watched in horror as one robber repeatedly hammered at the large front window until the glass finally gave way.





Another stood by clutching a large blue Ikea bag before the pair stuffed it with watches, bracelets and other jewellery from the smashed display.

Brave members of staff desperately tried to fend off the gang but were unable to stop them.

The thieves then fled on foot as stunned shoppers looked on, fearing for their own safety.

The robbery happened in Richmond, the picturesque London suburb where hit TV comedy Ted Lasso is filmed.

Detectives from the Met’s Flying Squad launched a major investigation, trawling through CCTV, carrying out forensic examinations and recovering a vehicle believed to be linked to the raid.



Their enquiries led officers to identify Mehmet, Ramsey and Clarke, who were arrested during a series of raids in Essex in March and April.

Body-worn camera footage released by police showed officers storming Ramsey’s home in the early hours of March 31 before handcuffing him.

Clarke was arrested after officers woke him while he was in bed during the same operation.



Mehmet was later detained while walking along a street in Basildon on April 8.

The three men, from Rochford, Harlow and Basildon respectively, all pleaded guilty to conspiracy to rob.

Despite the convictions, none of the stolen jewellery has ever been recovered.

Detective Superintendent Dan Mitchell, from the Met’s Flying Squad, said: “Robberies of this kind cause real concern for residents and businesses in the communities that are targeted. It’s they who feel the immediate impact.

“These sentences mark a significant step in what has been a detailed and determined investigation.



“I hope they demonstrate our commitment to tackling smash-and-grab robberies in London by going after those involved, wherever they are.

“The groups responsible should be under no illusion – we will pursue you relentlessly and hold you to account.”

The family-run jeweller, which has served Richmond for more than 45 years, previously thanked the public for rallying behind the business following the raid.

A spokesman for Gregory & Co said: “We’re a local, independent, family jewellers and have been in Richmond for more than 45 years.

“The public response to this incident has been overwhelming and we are grateful for the support and kindness we’ve received.



“We are reassured that overall, good outweighs the bad.”

News.title: Spain mobilises Army as stores & bars close after thousands of migrants storm border and at least 18 die on trip
News.content:
SPAIN has mobilised its army after thousands of migrants stormed a border crossing, causing terrified locals to close stores, restaurants and bars.

At least 18 people have died while trying to swim to Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in northern Africa that is seeing waves of migrants arriving on its shores.



Local authorities urged the government to declare a national emergency as overwhelmed border guards struggled to deal with the influx.

It has prompted Madrid to mobilise army units to support the overrun Guardia Civil – who were still dealing with migrants arriving after nightfall.



Tanks and soldiers have been pictured taking the streets as they shut down to the border to Morocco.

Spanish President Pedro Sanchez is also due to visit the embattled enclave later today.



Local business owners opted to keep their shutters down as thousands flood the city centre.

Residents are reportedly fearing for their safety amid a high risk of looting and riots.

The President of Ceuta, Juan Jesus Vivas, was quick to declare a total humanitarian and social emergency.

He said: “In the past few days more than 1,500 migrants, both adults and minors, have come to Ceuta by sea.



“The reception centres are saturated – there is no more room for anyone in them and according to yesterday’s figures the number of people entering is more than 200 a day.”

Spain’s soft-touch Supreme Court has come under fire for ruling that migrants who arrive by sea should not be subject to immediate expulsion as they are not crossing a physical land border.

The decision has been exploited by people-smuggling gangs and brought with it a wave of undocumented migration.

In response, Italian PM Giorgia Meloni declared she is prepared to ban Spain from the Schengen area.



She wrote on X: “The images coming from Ceuta are striking and demonstrate, once again, that uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders.

“We are convening the relevant bodies, and following these meetings, we are prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.

“On illegal immigration, we will not yield an inch: defending the borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriations will continue to be the line of this Government.”



Spain‘s socialist government stands out for its pro-migration stance.

It has recently launched a scheme to provide legal status to 500,000 undocumented migrants and received a huge influx of applications.

Shocking video from yesterday’s explosion of arrivals in Ceuta showed crowds of people, mainly Moroccans, rushing across the sand attempting to make it to the road.

The majority are young men but several whole families, including young children, can also be seen.

They had managed to jump over the border fence separating the city from Morocco, according to Spanish state news agency EFE.



Some could be heard chanting “Viva Espana!” – Long Live Spain – as they walked past.

The Moroccan government also promised it would work “faithfully and permanently with Spain” in regards to the ongoing crisis.

They said: “Moroccan security forces are preventing the arrival of numerous people who are trying to reach Ceuta from Morocco.”

Morocco and Spain have reportedly agreed to return migrants who entered Ceuta during the latest surge, according to Hespress.

Vivas said 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months with several washing up to shore in Ceuta.



He has warned the humanitarian crisis will only worsen while migrant centers are so full as hundreds of people will be forced to sleep on the streets.

He added that housing units for minors were now operating at 2,400 per cent capacity.

Back in 2021, 8,000 migrants swam from Morocco into Ceuta over a few days.

The arrivals also included the largest ever number of migrants in a single day, thought to be around 6,000.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ceuta residents had locked themselves indoors as the army rounded up migrants fleeing Morocco, La Vanguardia reported.



Hundreds of migrants risk injuries or even death every year while trying to jump over fences, hide inside vehicles or by swimming around breakwaters that extend into the Mediterranean Sea.

News.title: Famous mountain climber who starred in Netflix doc & has MBE goes missing after massive avalanche atop peak
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ICE HORROR Famous mountain climber who starred in Netflix doc & has MBE goes missing after massive avalanche atop peak

A WORLD-famous mountaineer who starred in a hit Netflix documentary has gone missing after a huge avalanche tore through one of the world’s tallest peaks.

Nirmal Purja MBE, known as Nimsdai, is among ten climbers missing after the avalanche struck Pakistan’s Broad Peak on Thursday afternoon.



The 43-year-old former Royal Marine was leading a team on the 26,414ft mountain – the world’s 12th highest – when disaster hit.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan said the group has been out of contact for several hours as a desperate search and rescue mission gets under way.





Five Nepalese climbers, led by Purja, and Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, from Hunza, are among those believed to have vanished.

Rescuers are racing to reach the remote mountainside as officials scramble to deploy helicopters and other emergency resources.



Major General Irfan Arshad, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan, said the organisation was working closely with government officials to coordinate the rescue effort.

He said every effort was being made to send helicopters and other available relief resources to the area as quickly as possible.

Broad Peak stands 8,051 metres above sea level and is regarded as one of the toughest mountains in the world to climb.

Purja is one of the world’s best-known mountaineers.

He shot to global fame after climbing all 14 of the world’s mountains higher than 8,000 metres in just 189 days, smashing the previous record.



The astonishing feat was documented in the Netflix film “14 Peaks: Nothing is Impossible”.

Before becoming a professional climber, Purja served for six years in the elite Gurkha regiment before spending a decade with the UK’s Special Boat Service.

In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by Queen Elizabeth II for exceptional military service in high-risk environments.

The search for Purja and the other missing climbers remains ongoing.

News.title: Crete wildfires live: Rethymno in flames amid mass evacuations on Greek islands
News.content:
A state of emergency has been declared in parts of Crete and elsewhere in Greece as firefighters battle intense wildfires, with crews on Crete unable to use aircraft to fight the flames because of hurricane-force winds

A state of emergency has been declared in parts of Crete and elsewhere in Greece as firefighters battle intense wildfires.

The blazes in the Rethymno region of southern Crete have scorched around 4,500 hectares since Wednesday. Hurricane-force winds - which reached speeds of up to 125km/h (78mph) yesterday - grounded firefighting aircraft and hampered efforts to contain the flames. Firefighters resumed operations on the ground today without the use of aircraft.

Thousands of people, including tourists, were evacuated yesterday, though some have since been allowed to return to their homes. Fires are also raging on Paros, Andros and Kalymnos islands, parts of the Peloponnese and western mainland Greece.

The fresh outbreaks in Greece, Portugal and Turkey come after devastating wildfires tore through parts of France and Spain, leaving a trail of destruction.

News.title: Scientists uncover traces of two mysterious 'ghost' ancestors in human DNA
News.content:
Scientists uncover traces of two mysterious 'ghost' ancestors in human DNA

The new findings suggest modern-day humans are the result of thousands of years of interbreeding between various groups of primates called hominis - but only one survives today: Homo sapiens

View 2 Images (Image: Getty Images)

Scientists have identified traces of ‘ghost ancestors’ in human DNA to help explain our genetic makeup.

‌



Researchers found DNA from two unknown groups of hominis, the group of primates which include homo sapiens and neanderthals. One originates from Africa around 50,000 years ago, while the other ‘super archaic’ hominis lineage is much older at 1.8 million years old.

‌



It’s thought they interbred with Denisovans, another group of hominis which have since died out, like neanderthals. They mixed DNA in Eurasia and Denisovans shared the ‘super-archaic’ DNA with homo sapiens thousands of years later.

‌



It’s thought there is a similar amount of ‘ghost DNA’ in modern-day humans to that of neanderthals, around 1 percent.

"We discovered that about 2 percent of the modern human genome is from archaic hominins," Yulin Zhang, one of the UC Berkeley researchers who made the breakthrough, said.

‌



"In the case of the ghost lineage, modern-day Africans and non-African populations both inherited similar amounts of ghost ancestry. Each individual has about 0.5 percent to 1 percent of their genome inherited from this ghost lineage."

View 2 Images Humans share similar amount of ghost DNA to that of neanderthals, with one on display in London

Arjun Biddanda, a postdoctoral researcher at Johns Hopkins University and a co-first author of the study, told Phys.Org : "The super-archaic finding is particularly exciting because it reveals genetic contributions from a human lineage that lived over a million years ago, despite the absence of any sequenced DNA from that population."

Article continues below

It was previously thought ‘ghost DNA’ existed in modern-day African people, but the research has found it in equal measure among Africans and non-Africans, suggesting much of the interbreeding took place before homo sapiens began exploring beyond the continent.

The findings also underscore theories that modern-day homo sapiens are made up of a mix of extinct hominis genes, suggesting the various groups interbred for thousands of years to produce the humans we see today.

News.title: Suffolk fire live: Wildfire near nuclear plant burns for third day as crews work tirelessly overnight
News.content:
Wildlife habitats devastated by the 'utterly sickening' wildfire at Dunwich Heath could reportedly take up to 25 years to recover

A massive wildfire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk has devastated wildlife habitats which could now reportedly take up to 25 years to recover - as multiple crews continue to tackle flames.

The area along the Suffolk coast went up in flames at about 5pm on Wednesday before engulfing an area equivalent to about 140 football pitches near Sizewell B nuclear power plant . It included parts of the RSPB's Minsmere nature reserve, which is home to rare birds, including Dartford warblers, nightjars, stonechats as well as reptiles such as adders, common lizards and slow worms

Adam Rowlands, the Suffolk area manager for the RSPB, told the BBC some of the habitat "will take five, 10, 25 years to come back to what it looked like before the fire broke out yesterday afternoon".

Some 200 caravans were evacuated from the path of the blaze yesterday, with holidaymakers woken up by officials banging on their doors. At least 12 fire engines were at the scene overnight tackling smaller fires that continued to break out.

On Thursday afternoon, an EDF spokesperson said the fire was "not affecting operations at Sizewell B power station".

News.title: UK woman first in world to receive pioneering cancer therapy
News.content:
UK woman first in world to receive pioneering cancer therapy

Tracy Tomlinson has already beaten the odds to stay alive

View 4 Images Tracy Tomlinson has spent more than five years living with deadly ovarian cancer (Image: Family/PA)

A woman with advanced ovarian cancer has become the first patient in the world to receive a pioneering new therapy.

‌



Tracy Tomlinson, 58, was given the drug at the Christie NHS Foundation Trust in Manchester as part of a clinical trial evaluating a new type of treatment for several types of cancer. The therapy, known as ZI-MA4-1, will be tested on people with ovarian cancer, lung cancer, sarcomas and head and neck cancer in a trial led by the Christie, with a site also at the Royal Marsden in London.

‌



Many people in the study have few other options for survival. Mrs Tomlinson, from Chadderton in Greater Manchester, has already beaten the odds in staying alive, having undergone surgery and several rounds of chemotherapy since she was diagnosed in 2020.

‌



The new therapy works by combining two powerful methods in fighting cancer. Firstly, it harnesses the body’s natural killer (NK) cells, which are specialist immune cells that destroy abnormal ones.

Secondly, T-cell receptors (TCRs) on the cells are engineered to recognise and target tumours producing a protein called Mage-A4. Mage-A4 is found in several types of cancer and experts believe it is an ideal target for attacking abnormal cells.

Unlike some personalised treatments, ZI-MA4-1 is designed as an “off-the-shelf” therapy that uses immune cells from donors. The treatment is manufactured in advance from donor cells rather than being individually tailored to each patient, with hundreds of doses produced from a single manufacturing batch.

‌



View 4 Images Tracy Tomlinson (Image: Family/PA)

Experts believe this could mean advanced cell therapies are available to more patients more quickly, and at a cheaper cost. Mrs Tomlinson was diagnosed with ovarian cancer that had spread shortly before Christmas 2020 and immediately underwent treatment.

By summer 2021, scans showed no evidence of disease but, a year later, the cancer returned. Despite further rounds of treatment and 48 chemotherapy infusions, her cancer kept coming back.

‌



The former Civil Service manager told the Press Association she was diagnosed as stage 3C, which means there were cancer growths spreading into the peritoneum of the body. She currently has a tumour between the liver and kidney as well as small tumours elsewhere.

She said: “They’ve got rid of the cancer twice, but then it came back about two-and-a-half years ago and we’ve never seemed to get rid of it since then. The chemotherapy has shrunk it, but when treatment stops, it has come back.

“It is a lot to live with and there’s been ups and downs – there’s been elation, there’s been disappointment and bits in between. But I try very, very hard to remain very positive. Every day that I wake up is a positive. You’ve got to have hope.”

‌



Mrs Tomlinson said that in her working life she was target-driven and set herself very high standards.

“But you can’t control cancer,” she said. “What I can control is how I look at it, how I deal with it, and trying to eat healthily and taking the positives in everything.

“And I’ve learned to appreciate the smallest of things that we take for granted – and the people around you and what they mean to you. Also, the beauty of outside and the trees and the colour of the trees and the birds singing.

‌



“We just go from A to B, don’t we? Busy, busy, busy. But we never slow down and take in the wonder of what’s around us.

“I often think, ‘I’m still here’, and that’s helped me think, ‘Why can’t I still be here in 10 years?’, ‘Why can’t I still be here in 15 years?’

“And I believe taking all the treatments offered to me is helping me kick that can a bit further down the road. I don’t want to go anywhere. I’ve still got a lot of things I want to do and things I want to achieve.”

‌



View 4 Images Tracy Tomlinson has become the first patient in the world to receive a pioneering new therapy (Image: Family/PA)

Mrs Tomlinson said husband Paul, whom she married in 2022, was her “rock” and she is also close to her son Harry, 28. Last year, she was referred to the Christie’s early phase clinical trials team for extensive screening, and learned she was a suitable candidate for the Zima-101 clinical trial.

“I decided almost straight away that I was going to go for it,” she said. “Then afterwards you think, ‘Am I doing the right thing?’, because it is a little bit scary being the first person in the world to have the treatment.”

‌



She has had three infusions of the therapy, with the option of another one depending on what scans show.

“If it benefits me, absolutely fantastic,” she said. “But if it benefits other people in the future, that’s important too. I don’t want to have gone through everything I’ve gone through for nothing. I want to feel like I have made a difference.”

Professor Fiona Thistlethwaite, consultant medical oncologist at the Christie, said: “While this is an early-stage study primarily focused on safety, it represents an exciting step forward in efforts to develop new treatment options for people like Tracy with advanced solid tumours. We hope the knowledge gained will help shape future cancer treatments and ultimately improve outcomes for patients.”

‌



Dr Jon Lim, consultant medical oncologist in advanced immunotherapy and cell therapy at the Christie, told PA: “What’s very exciting about this is that these are essentially not kind of antibody-based, but living cells. These are live immune cells that are infused in hundreds of millions back to the patient, and the idea of this is that it is a little bit more targeted.

“The reason this is very interesting is because this is the first of its kind globally in this approach, where it’s taking donor immune cells, manipulating or engineering them, and putting them into the recipient. Tracy is essentially getting somebody else’s immune cells that have been engineered to ‘see’ her cancer.

“We’re very excited. This is a novel approach in the cell therapy space. We are also really showcasing what we can do in the UK.”

‌



View 4 Images Tracy was given the first dose of ZI-MA4-1 at the Christie NHS Foundation Trust as part of a clinical trial (Image: Family/PA)

Namir Hassan, chief executive of Norwegian firm Zelluna, which makes ZI-MA4-1, said Mrs Tomlinson’s first dose is a “landmark moment”, adding: “It represents the moment when years of research moved beyond the laboratory and into the clinic, offering a new potential treatment option for patients facing advanced cancers with limited alternatives.”

Only around 15% of women survive ovarian cancer for five years or more after they are diagnosed.

Article continues below

Dr Diana Hernandez, director of immune and advanced therapies at Anthony Nolan, said: “NK cells have huge potential as off-the-shelf therapies, and this trial takes us one step closer to a wider application of engineered NK cells in the targeted treatment of cancers. At Anthony Nolan we have long seen the potential of cellular therapies like this to transform the lives of patients with blood cancer. Today’s research represents exciting progress for patients with solid tumours to benefit from these promising therapies.”

News.title: Hamas to 'completely disarm' in Gaza as Trump claims 'historic' step towards peace
News.content:
Hamas to 'completely disarm' in Gaza as Trump claims 'historic' step towards peace

US President Donald Trump announced an agreement had been reached for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza as well as the withdrawal of Israeli troops.

View Image Hamas is set to "completely disarm" in Gaza (Image: AP)

Hamas is set to "completely disarm" in Gaza under an agreement Donald Trump has described as a "historic" step towards peace.

The deal would see the militant group lay down its weapons as part of a phased process.

News.title: Sainsbury's to sell Argos business for £120million
News.content:
Sainsbury's to sell Argos business for £120million

The deal will see Argos stores and collection points sold to Swift Partners, a new company which has been set up for this acquisition

View Image Sainsbury's is selling Argos (Image: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images)

Sainsburys has agreed to sell Argos for at least £120million in order to focus on its core food business.

‌



The deal will see Argos stores and collection points sold to Swift Partners, a new company which has been set up for this acquisition.

‌



But the supermarket said it is "business as usual" for Argos, which will continue to trade as normal. Argos operates through standalone stores, stores inside Sainsbury's, online delivery and collection points. In addition, Swift will buy Argos' pet insurance business and product warranty cover.

‌



It will also acquire Sainsbury's distribution centre located in Daventry and Sainsbury's sourcing offices located in Shanghai and Hong Kong. The deal is expected to complete in February 2027.

We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

Argos was bought by Sainsbury's for £1.4billion in 2016, with the supermarket going on to close hundreds of standalone stores, located largely in high streets or retail parks.

‌



All physical shops and online services in the Republic of Ireland permanently shut down in June 2023.

Simon Roberts, Chief Executive of J Sainsbury plc, said: "Swift brings retail leadership, operational expertise, technology capability and long-term investment, alongside a deep commitment and belief in the future potential for Argos customers and colleagues.

"I would like to thank Argos colleagues for all of their commitment and hard work. Today is an important next step in building the strongest future for Argos and I would like to reassure our colleagues, customers and suppliers that it's business as usual."

‌



Swift Partners is made up of retail specialists, including former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook, former Morrisons chief operating officer Trevor Strain, and backed by Matt Truman and his retail investment and advisory firm, True Capital.

Sainsbury’s will get cash proceeds of at least £120million from the sale, with a £70million up front payment when the deal completes.

Mr Pennycook said: "We hold Argos senior management in high regard and plan to build on its strengths - bringing additional experience and skills to complement and augment the existing team.

Article continues below

"We see clear potential to strengthen Argos's customer proposition, digital capabilities and nationwide reach."

News.title: Olivia Attwood takes another swipe at ex Bradley Dack's girlfriend despite manager's plea
News.content:
Olivia Attwood takes another swipe at ex Bradley Dack's girlfriend despite manager's plea

Olivia Attwood has made another dig at her ex Bradley Dack's girlfriend Emily following reports that the footballer is back with his ex

View 3 Images Olivia Attwood has made another dig (Image: olivia_attwood/Instagram)

Olivia Attwood has made another dig at her ex Bradley Dack's girlfriend as their feud intensifies.

‌



The former Love Island star shocked her fans when she launched a series of attacks on Bradley Dack's new girlfriend as she blasted her for grabbing her "10 minutes of fame". Bradley is seemingly back with his ex Emily after the pair have been spotted out and about together and heading back to his flat.

‌



Despite being in a happy relationship with Pete Wicks, Olivia has fired back at Emily on multiple occasions, including saying that "they all want their 10 mins now," raging: "These people get tangled in their own web of lies," with her manager quickly advising her to be the "bigger person" and stay quiet.

‌



In her latest dig, when one TikTok user made a post that read: "You’re either an Emily or an Olivia and I know who I’d rather be," Olivia was quick to jump in the comments, adding: "OMG [crying emoji]."

3 View 3 Images Olivia is now with her friend Pete Wicks (Image: p_wicks01/Instagram) 3 View 3 Images Bradley Dack and Olivia Attwood split earlier this year (Image: Lia Toby, Getty Images)

‌



In a string of posts, an angry Olivia fumed over Bradley's new woman. "These people get tangled in their own web of lies," she raged. "All you have to do is sit back and wait. Took seven months of people trying to make me think I was crazy and they are all coming out the woodwork now." Another post read: "They all want their 10 mins now."

In a fiery third post, Olivia continued: "I have definitely beat up myself over my poor judgement over the last decade, but I guess I could of spent 10 years as the bit on the side/professional bench warmer, so silver linings I guess."

In a video shared on her Instagram story Olivia later told fans to prepare as she was ready to share some fiery messages. Minutes later she returned to social media, revealing she'd had a strict warning from her manager.

‌



“The screenshots are on pause because my manager wanted me to be the bigger person,” she told fans, as she wandered around Selfridges with a friend and bought some expensive shoes for a spontaneous night out.

Olivia is now dating her long-time friend Pete Wicks, who recently opened up about his nerves about hard launching his romance.

"The thought process was, 'What would Liv like?' We'd spoken about it and I thought, 'Ah f**k it', you know. Let's go and do it. Obviously the first photo had to be of me and Liv, and all I really cared about was that I didn’t embarrass her," he said.

‌



"I would love to take full credit for [the music], but it was suggested by Instagram. But yeah, just simple. Just, 'There we go'. Now it's out it's fine, we're good."

When Olivia split from Bradley earlier this year, she claimed that she was "lied to" and "cheated on multiple times". In a statement, she wrote: "I have stood by Brad for the last ten years during which he lied and cheated on me multiple times. The breakdown of our relationship is because of this.

"I was in love with him and the potential I saw in him and wanted always to help him try to be the best version of himself - as I did for 10 years - covering up. Lying to my family and friends. Arranging therapy. Believing the grovelling apologies."

Article continues below

She added: "I of course now feel like a f***ing idiot. (Especially as more things come to the surface) I never wanted to say any of this.. I find the whole situation utterly humiliating."

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow mayors of English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

The Conservatives said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

The power to raise and control tax revenues is highly centralised in the UK, making the country an outlier by international standards.

The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external, a global policy forum.

That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%), and the US (45.7%).

As it stands, mayors of strategic authorities in England receive most of their funding from central government grants.

During his time as Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham pushed for greater control over tax revenue, rather than having to rely on government grants.

The UK government had already been exploring whether a share of revenue from national taxes could be distributed to metro mayors, before Burnham became prime minister earlier this month.

But in a major speech on devolution in June, Burnham said he would "oversee the biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen" if he became prime minister.

Burnham has put devolution at the heart of his plan for government, arguing that metro mayors are best placed to boost economic growth across the country.

News.title: Satellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscape
News.content:
Satellite imagery shows the toll taken on the UK landscape from this year's long hot summer.

BBC Verify analysis of satellite data shows where in the UK has been most affected by heatwaves and a lack of rain.

We can see parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.

Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and have an impact on agriculture and food supplies.

Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.

News.title: British man accused of spying on Cyprus RAF base for Iran
News.content:
A British man has been arrested on suspicion of spying on a UK military base in Cyprus on behalf of the Iranian military.

Rashad Sultanov, 44, of Islington, north London, is accused of carrying out "hostile surveillance" on RAF Akrotiri and sharing information with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Sultanov, who also holds Azerbaijani citizenship, was arrested by Cypriot police on 17 July and is in custody pending extradition proceedings.

The Crown Prosecution Service has said he will be charged under the National Security Act - the first time an alleged offence under the 2023 law has been investigated in an overseas territory.

The UK has maintained a permanent base at Akrotiri since the 1950s and RAF operations to shoot down Iranian missiles and drones have been launched from there in recent months.

The investigation, which was led by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London, focused on alleged spying between 11 May 2025 and 22 June 2025.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of CTP London, said: "This case shows we are able to use the National Security Act overseas when British military bases are allegedly targeted by hostile state activity.

"A huge amount of partnership work has been carried out between British and Cypriot law enforcement agencies.

"We continue to work with colleagues from the CPS, National Crime Agency and Cypriot authorities as extradition proceedings progress."

News.title: Anthropic's Claude AI escapes tests to hack three organisations
News.content:
US technology firm Anthropic says its artificial intelligence (AI) models hacked into the systems of three organisations during a cybersecurity test due to an error that gave them access to the internet.

It comes just days after rival OpenAI said that its models had breached the systems of other companies, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.

The announcement prompted Anthropic to check whether its own models had carried out similar attacks. It says it uncovered three cases that have since been reported to the affected companies.

Anthropic, which did not name the organisations, urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.

Anthropic said in a statement, external that it reviewed more than 140,000 tests to find evidence that Claude - its family of AI models - could access the internet from testing environments that were designed to be sealed off.

The tests include so-called "capture-the-flag" evaluations in which Claude was tasked with obtaining information by breaching other systems - a common way that experts assess a model's hacking capabilities.

A "misconfiguration" on systems run by Anthropic and its testing partner left the models with live internet access, allowing them to breach other systems, the San Francisco-based firm said.

Anthropic said the earliest incidents date back to April and that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."

Neither Anthropic nor the organisations that were breached had noticed the intrusions at the time.

Anthropic said it could have reviewed its records more thoroughly and added that the findings gave the firm "cautious optimism" that such risks can be overcome with more investment and tighter measures.

"The broader lesson is not necessarily that AI has developed a fundamentally new attack capability," cyber security expert David Allott told the BBC.

"Instead, it is that AI agents can combine capabilities, obtain credentials and system access to take actions autonomously, while adapting scope and scale at machine speed," he added.

The incidents come as tech firms pour billions of dollars into developing AI agents that can independently perform tasks ranging from research and customer support to cybersecurity.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its core food business.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company which has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

Under the terms of the deal, Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for customers, staff, and suppliers. The deal is expected to complete next February.

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal comes a decade after Sainsbury's bought Argos â as well as Homebase, Habitat, and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â for Â£1.3bn.

Retail analyst Clive Black said he had always questioned whether Argos was "wholly aligned" with Sainsbury's grocery business, describing the supermarket group's attempt to sell Argos as "challenging and prolonged".

News.title: Situation is stabilising, say crews tackling Suffolk wildfire
News.content:
The fire service said power had also been restored to 111 of 116 properties that had their supply cut off.

A helicopter on site will remain in use into Friday, with each drop unloading 1,000 litres of seawater on to the blaze.

A spokesperson for the Sizewell B nuclear power station, about three miles (5km) from the fire, said it was monitoring the "dynamic situation".

Homes and a holiday caravan park were evacuated after the fire broke out and there are fears for rare birds and wildlife whose home is the heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere.

Dartford warblers, nightjars and stonechats, along with reptiles such as adders, common lizards and slow worms, are among the species found there.

The "large-scale, wind-driven" fire was declared a major incident on Thursday morning, due to the size and complexity of the blaze, which was helped by south-westerly winds.

On Thursday evening, Suffolk's chief fire officer, Jon Lacey, said difficult terrain and limited access routes were making it hard for crews to reach some areas of the wildfire.

He confirmed that approximately 100 to 150 people had been evacuated from their accommodation.

An update on the fire service's website said it was being supported by firefighters from neighbouring brigades, with engines also being sent from London.

"We have also requested additional national support, including wildfire specialist appliances, officers, and tactical advisers," it said.

"Around 50 people have received support through the rest centre, which remains open.

"We expect the response to continue for at least the next 48 hours."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to give the fire service "all the support it needs" to tackle the "very serious" heathland blaze.

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner praised firefighters for their "skill and dedication and bravery".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for Burnham to host an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss the outbreak of wildfires in Britain, including in Suffolk.

News.title: Drought conditions may worsen before improving as little rain in sight
News.content:
Conditions in the most parched areas of the United Kingdom could worsen before they improve, according to the latest forecasts.

The coming days will offer little relief to the areas that need it most, including eastern, central and southern England, and the entirety of Wales.

Meanwhile, August as a whole is showing a trend towards warmer and drier-than-average conditions.

It comes as Natural Resources Wales (NRW) extended its drought declaration to the entirety of the country on Thursday, adding that the high temperatures were causing the natural environment to "deteriorate".

It follows a similar announcement from the Environment Agency on Wednesday which plunged more than half of England into drought conditions.

News.title: What your summer reading list says about you
News.content:
You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the Ãcole Normale SupÃ©rieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

Epic other-world adventures (action, adventure, science fiction, dystopian/post-apocalyptic, fantasy)

Everyday life and human relationships (comedy, romantic, drama, family, musical)

Threat and danger (true crime, crime/mystery/thriller, horror)

Facts and histories (documentary, biography, historical)

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

News.title: Thames Water boss says leakage targets 'not realistic'
News.content:
Water companies have performance commitments on issues such as leakage.

It is illegal to release raw sewage into rivers and seas during "normal" weather conditions, but firms are allowed to do so when it rains heavily, to prevent homes being flooded.

Thames is the UK's largest water company, supplying water and wastewater services to 16 million customers across London and parts of southern England.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Weston said the company treats 4.3 billion litres of waste a day, and "99.5% of the time" it gets treated successfully, although "sometimes something goes wrong".

"We want to do better when it comes to pollutions," he said, but added, "the targets that the company is expected to make are not realistic.

"[For example], we have to hit a certain level of leakage, but it is so far in excess of what we are capable of doing, I think anyone would be capable of doing, however much money you invested, that it is not going to be achievable."

The chance of getting to zero pollution was "very, very slim", he added.

Ofwat told the BBC: "With around a fifth of water put into supply still lost through leakage, companies must deliver on the commitments they have been funded to achieve.

"Water company targets are intended to be ambitious and drive better outcomes for customers and the environment."

A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said: "[We] and the public expect Thames Water to comply with the law," adding that the agency would continue to hold companies to account where performance falls short.

James Wallace, chief executive of campaign group River Action, said: "Thames Water's tactics of opacity and deflection fool no-one. Telling the public to save water while this wasteful profit-obsessed corporation leaks 570 million litres of treated drinking water every day is offensive.

"There is nothing 'realistic' about accepting sewage pollution as inevitable. The choice is simple: keep propping up a failed privatised financial model, or put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it as a public utility serving customers, rivers and the public."

News.title: MP Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
News.content:
The long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.

In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.

Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning".

East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.

Her husband David Taylor, was arrested along with two other men. All three have been released on police bail, which in May was extended until August.

Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".

She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."

News.title: Elderly victim of 'cruel' carer can't be left alone after being 'traumatised'
News.content:
An 81-year-old whose "cruel" carer was jailed after being caught on camera abusing her cannot be left alone because she is "traumatised," her daughter has said.

Louise Harris was given a three-month sentence after CCTV filmed her drunkenly screaming "I hope you die in your sleep... you horrible cow" at Elizabeth Anne Shipton in Pontardawe, Neath Port Talbot.

Elizabeth's daughter Tracy Faram Shipton called Harris's actions "horrific" and said her sentence for ill treatment and criminal damage was "laughable".

Despite this, the family is unable to appeal against it as, under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, external, the attorney general can only refer specific qualifying crimes to the Court of Appeal.

Harris, 42, was filmed on the family's video surveillance system, which was originally installed so Tracy and her brother could monitor their late father John in case he fell while caring for Elizabeth.

She had originally been charged with attempted robbery - a crime which would have qualified for sentencing to be appealed by the victim's family - but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) dropped that charge.

"Mum can't be left on her own at all now," Tracy added.

A CPS spokesman said: "We keep all cases under review and on this occasion concluded that our legal test was not met, as there was insufficient evidence to prosecute the defendant with attempted robbery and theft.

"We have written to the victim to explain our decision in more detail."

News.title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
News.content:
Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.

In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"

This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.

"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."

He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."

"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."

Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."

In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.

"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.

"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."

The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.

Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".

Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".

Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.

"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."

Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" - production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.

Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.

In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.

The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.

Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.

If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

The levy is due to be replaced in 2030 by another windfall tax, which operators prefer because it's only triggered when prices are high and falls back when they are low.

News.title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
News.content:
The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.

While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".

Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.

The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than Â£1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.

The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year.

Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.

The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.

That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund
News.content:
This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in March.

Reparative justice has been one of the themes running through the Ghana leg of this trip.

At Cape Coast Castle, which came under British control in the 1660s, Dame Sarah was shown dungeons where slaves were held, and the so-called "door of no return" through which they were forced on to ships.

The archbishop said: "You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in and the way that they were treated.

"It completely throws you off balance and brings home the evil that was transatlantic slavery."

Above the dungeons sits a chapel, which she said was a "stark illustration of the way the church was involved in the slave trade".

The Church of England has previously apologised for its associations with the slave trade.

Its missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

News.title: British Airways flight called mayday on approach to Heathrow
News.content:
A British Airways flight issued a "mayday" distress call on its approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month, according to a statement from France's accident investigation authority.

The call was made on an Airbus A320 flying from Dusseldorf airport in Germany on 6 July following two stall warnings on the aircraft, before it landed without further incident.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident".

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

The French Air Safety Investigation Authority, the BEA, said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet - which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

The BEA website attributed the statement to the AAIB, but the AAIB would not confirm it was from them.

They issued the following statement: "The AAIB is investigating a serious incident involving a commercial aircraft which occurred on 6 July on approach to Heathrow airport."

It said the investigation would be a correspondence investigation, meaning that no team would be sent to carry out field investigations.

Aviation safety investigator David Gleave said there are different forms of mayday calls, and to send an urgency message was "not unusual".

"You could have sick passengers on board who need urgent medical attentionâ¦ so it's up to the captains' discretion as to what they call, but its very unusual for it to be a significant failure on board the aeroplane."

News.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
News.content:
The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action.

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

News.title: World Cup boycott latest: Infantino refuses to back down after Uefa say they’ll refuse to play in Fifa tournaments
News.content:
Inside Uefa’s extraordinary World Cup boycott plans – and what Fifa might do next

Fifa has hit back at Uefa’s boycott of the World Cup and plans to press on with its proposals to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors.

In a statement on Friday, Fifa insisted that “nobody is selling football” and confirmed that it will continue its consultation period ahead of a vote on 19 September.

On Thursday, Uefa announced that it would boycott the World Cup and all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its major tournaments to external investors are voted through.

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one,” a statement said following an emergency Uefa meeting. “We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

Meanwhile, Concacaf, the confederation representing 41 nations from North and Central America, along with the Caribbean, also made clear its opposition to Fifa’s plan, saying it “rejected the proposal”.

Franco Baresi, the legendary AC Milan defender and World Cup winner with Italy, has died at the age of 66.

Milan, the club Baresi represented for his entire 20-year career and won three Champions League titles with, announced his death on Friday morning.

No cause of death was given, but Baresi underwent surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule in August 2025 and had been receiving treatment.

His last public appearance at at Milan’s San Siro stadium in February, when he carried the torch into the opening ceremony for the Winger Olympics.

"The entire history of AC Milan is in tears," Milan said.

“Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan, is incredibly difficult. But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi’s memory. We must be strong and gather every bit of energy, even at this saddest of times.

“His example and integrity will be forever etched into the Club’s DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is. The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi’s family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own.”

The former Milan captain is widely regarded as one of the finest defenders in football history played 719 times for the club in 20 seasons as a professional.

During that time, Baresi won six Serie A crowns, with his first Scudetto coming as a teenager during the 1978-79 campaign and he lifted five further titles in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The defender also won three European Cups, two Intercontinental Cups and four Italian Supercups during his career and his contributions to Milan saw the club retire the number six jersey.

On the international stage, Baresi was part of the Italy squad which won the World Cup in 1982, as well as featuring in the 1994 World Cup, which ended in a penalty shootout defeat to Brazil in the final.

More follows
