World.title: Poland blames Russia for firing missile into its territory as Moscow unleashes deadly attack on Ukraine
World.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine —

A missile apparently fired by Russia landed deep inside Polish territory, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday, as Moscow launched deadly long-range attacks across Ukraine that killed at least eight people.

The missile landed and exploded about 90 kilometers (55 miles) into Polish territory early Thursday, leaving a massive crater in the middle of a field, local authorities said.

“We were prepared to shoot down the missile if it had continued its flight,” Tusk told an emergency government meeting, according to his office on X. “All indications suggest that it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile.”

Two NATO fighter jets, a NATO refueling aircraft, a Polish early warning aircraft and a Polish helicopter were deployed to counter the threat, a spokesperson for the alliance told CNN.

NATO will “continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory, General Alexus G. Grynkewich, the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, said in a statement to CNN.

Still, there are no reasons to think Poland was the intended target, Tusk said later when he visited the crater site, according to Reuters.

Poland had earlier reported scrambling fighter jets in response to a major Russian attack on Ukraine, which hit large swathes of the country, killed at least eight people, including children, and left dozens more injured or trapped under rubble.

Any potential Russian attack so deep inside a NATO member’s territory would risk being perceived as an escalation in Moscow’s yearslong war on Ukraine. It is not the first time Poland has reported a “Russian-made” missile landing inside its territory – but this one reached unusually far. In November 2022, one struck and killed two people but that incident was only 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) from the Ukrainian border.

The attacks come days after Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky traveled to the United States to again plead for more air defenses, as Russia fires more ballistic missiles into Ukraine and intensifies its air assaults on the country’s cities. As a result, more Ukrainian civilians have been killed this month than in any since April 2022. At the same time, Kyiv is emphasizing its ability to hit deep inside Russia, attacking Wildberries facilities, often described as “Russia’s Amazon,” across the border.

People take shelter inside a metro station during a Russian missile and drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday, July 30. Alina Smutko/Reuters

Deadly strikes in Ukraine

This wave of attacks killed at least eight people across the country, according to its foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, including six members of a single family.

In the village of Radushne, near Zelensky’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih, parents and four children were killed after a ballistic missile blew a family home “into smithereens,” Zelensky said. Two more children were pulled alive from the rubble, he added.

Two girls, aged 5 and 12, were among the four children killed, Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the southern Ukrainian city’s military administration, said on Telegram, calling it a “dark night.”

Graphic video from Radushne showed bodies strewn amid the rubble of a shattered building, with fires still burning.

Two unseen women could be heard speaking. “We’ve pulled one child out. There are still some lying over there,” one said.

“There are children here. There are many children,” the other said.

In Lviv, emergency workers rescued an injured 10-year-old boy, who was carried away on a stretcher, as they raced to save people trapped under rubble after an attack on a residential building. Dozens across the country were wounded.

Missile crater in Poland

The missile crashed in an undeveloped area near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia in Lublin province, Poland’s army said. Polish police said residents reported hearing a powerful blast.

Separately, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said a Russian cruise missile had “crossed into Poland as part of Russia’s massive strike against Ukraine” in a post to X.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it carried out a “massive strike using long-range precision weapons from land, air, and sea” as well as attack drones on military sites across Ukraine, in a statement posted to Telegram Thursday.

Poland’s army said the country’s air defenses observed at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine, which posed a potential threat to Polish airspace.

The attack damaged or destroyed dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities, Zelensky said on Telegram Thursday, and used more than 70 missiles and over 280 attack drones.

Ukraine intercepted more than 260 drones, according to Zelensky, in what he said was a commendable feat given a “critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners.”

On his way home on Wednesday, Zelensky stopped in the Polish city of Lublin – not far from the site of the next day’s crash – to meet with Tusk. The two leaders discussed “the outcomes of (Zelensky’s) visit to the United States and the security of Poland, Ukraine, and all of Europe,” according to a post to X by Tusk.

Poland has routinely scrambled jets in response to Russian attacks on western Ukraine, though they have rarely entered its territory. NATO fighter jets shot down multiple Russian drones that violated Polish airspace last September, denouncing Moscow for “absolutely dangerous behavior.”

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: Vice President urges Mpulungu residents to participate in electoral process
World.content:
Vice President, Mutale Nalumango, has called on Vyamba residents in Mpulungu district to participate actively in the electoral process by voting for the United Party for National Development (UPND) in the August General elections.

The Vice President expressed confidence in the party’s policies and leadership, encouraging voters to consider the development agenda that the UPND has laid out.

Speaking during a public meeting held at Vyamba Primary School Grounds today, Ms Nalumango assured supporters that the party is committed to improving the lives of Zambians and advancing economic growth.

She emphasized the importance of continuing the development agenda that the UPND has initiated, which has brought significant improvements to the lives of many Zambians.

The Vice President in her statement has since urged residents to rally behind the party and ensure that the country’s development trajectory remains on course.

Ms Nalumango continued that voting for the UPND party will ensure that there is continuity of various infrastructure development projects, including the construction of roads, bridges, and other public facilities.

She said this is because the UPND has also implemented policies aimed at improving the country’s economy, which has led to increased economic growth and reduced poverty levels.

Ms Nalumango has also issued a call to action for UPND supporters, urging them to maintain peace and unity across the country.

She emphasized the importance of peaceful conduct during the upcoming elections, highlighting that stability is crucial for national development.

And Mpulungu North Aspiring Member of Parliament, Jobicks Kalumba, assured the community that they will work together and ensure that meaningful development is seen in the district.

World.title: Ministries urged to strengthen communication for national development –Kawana
World.content:
Government has stressed that achieving national development requires effective and robust dissemination of information to ensure citizens actively participate in the country’s development agenda.

Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary, Thabo Kawana, says access to accurate and timely information is critical in enabling citizens to contribute to sustainable national development.

Mr Kawana says the Government’s target of increasing Zambia’s annual copper production to three million Metric Tonnes (MT) by 2030 can only be achieved if the public and key stakeholders are adequately informed about the strategies and interventions required to attain the target.

That the PS said this in Lusaka today, when he officially launched the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Digital Platform, the Podcast.

Mr Kawana commended the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development for investing in K1.2 million modern communication infrastructure to improve public access to information on the mining sector.

He said the establishment of the podcast demonstrates the ministry’s commitment to ensuring that the public receives accurate and credible information from experts and other stakeholders.

Mr Kawana further said the podcast will enhance implementation of the Access to Information Act by providing citizens with an easily accessible platform where they can obtain information on government policies, programmes and reforms in the mining sector.

He urged public institutions to allocate resources towards communication and public engagement to enhance transparency and improve service delivery.

Mr Kawana said members of the public will be able to search and access discussions on key issues such as local content regulations and other mining policies through the digital platform.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary, Kabeta Hapenga, disclosed that the Ministry has in recent years undertaken several policy and legal reforms whose success depends on effective communication with stakeholders.

Dr Hapenga noted that the podcast has been established to strengthen stakeholder engagement and improve communication on reforms taking place in the mining sector to significantly transform the country’s economy.

He further revealed that his Ministry has developed a stakeholder engagement strategy that outlines key audiences and the frequency of communication to ensure all stakeholders remain informed.

Dr Hapenga explained that the dedicated podcast platform will provide consistent updates on the Government’s mining policies, including the target of producing three million MT of copper annually and the implementation of local content regulations.

He noted that his Ministry plays a central role in Zambia’s economic transformation and therefore requires continuous engagement with traditional leaders, mining companies, investors and members of the public.

Dr Hapenga said the launch of the podcast marks an important milestone in the ministry’s efforts to promote transparency, public awareness and stakeholder participation in the development of Zambia’s mining sector.

The official launch of the podcast was witnessed by senior government officials from the two ministries and as well as ZANIS Director, Ms Loyce Saili.

World.title: UNICEF donates K2 Million for detection of viral haemorrhagic fevers
World.content:
UNICEF has donated Two Million Kwacha worth of infection prevention supplies and water, sanitation and hygiene equipment, aimed at strengthening detection of viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Ebola.

Speaking during the handover ceremony in Lusaka, Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary for Technical Services, Kennedy Lishimpi, clarified that the donation design is driven by preparedness, rather than reacting to threats as they emerge.

Dr Lishimpi said the donation will enhance the ministry’s ability to address current public health challenges and remain vigilant and prepared to prevent diseases such as Ebola from crossing the borders and affecting the citizens.

“We are choosing to act ahead of potential threats rather than react after they emerge, we are fully aware of the devastating impact that infectious disease outbreaks can have on nations, communities, and health systems,” he said.

Dr Lishimpi also disclosed that UNICEF is yet to donate 150 Ambulance vehicles by the end of September, out of which 50 are already in the country and a consignment of 200 vaccine refrigerators.

Meanwhile, UNICEF Country Representative, Saja Abdullah, said investing in preparedness before an emergency, will ensure that health workers are protected, communities safeguarded and that children continue to receive essential services they need before a crisis.

Dr Abdullah added that availability of essential items will ensure that health workers can respond quickly, provide safe care and contain any potential outbreak timely and effectively.

She added that the donation is a reflection of the strong partnership shared by both parties.

World.title: KGS supports over 257, 000 vulnerable girls
World.content:
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Permanent Secretary for Administration, Margaret Miyoba, has appreciated the Keeping Girls in School and beyond initiative that has supported over 257, 000 vulnerable girls since inception in 2016.

Ms Miyoba says by September 2026, the government will scale up the programme to 116 districts by adding 21 more districts to the existing 95 districts due to the positive impact the project has on the vulnerable girl child.

That she said this during the 2026 Annual Keeping Girls in School and Beyond Academic Symposium in Luangwa District held under the theme,” Empowering Girls: Creating leaders of tomorrow”.

She explained that the government is implementing the Girls’ Education and Women Empowerment and Livelihood for Human Capital (GEWEL II) across all the ten Provinces of Zambia with support from the World Bank and other cooperating partners, through the Multi-Dollar Trust Fund.

“The KGS programme has seen more than 30, 000 vulnerable girls completing their secondary education and three thousand from these have been awarded tertiary education support scholarships with 150 completing their tertiary education in readiness for transitioning into the world of work”, she explained.

Ms Miyoba encouraged the learners to appreciate the KGS Academic Symposium because it promotes sharing of best practices on enhancing academic excellence among KGS implementing schools so as to contribute to the development of human capital for national development.

Luangwa District Commissioner, Luke Chikani, thanked the government for the free education that has seen over 14, 489 learners in school in 2026 compared to the 9, 456 learners in Luangwa District in 2021.

Mr Chikani said this policy has increased opportunities for learners from disadvantaged families to access boarding facilities, following the reduction of the fees to K1000.

“These achievements reaffirm the Government’s commitment to ensuring that every child, regardless of their socio-economic background, has access to quality education”, Mr Chikani said.

Meanwhile, District Education Board Secretary, Motive Kampelya, explained that the district has 31 vulnerable girls fully sponsored under the KGS in different universities and colleges.

Mr Kampelya said with much academic encouragement given to the girl children, the district has recorded an increase in the pass rate from 72.85 percent in 2024 to 81.14 percent in 2025 becoming the best performing in the Lusaka Province.

“Guest of Honor, allow me to boast that Luangwa District scooped the first position at Grade Twelve level in Lusaka Province and this achievement can only be attributed to the good education policies initiated by the government”, he proudly remarked.

World.title: President Hichilema pledges improved road network in Mwandi
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has promised the people of Mwandi district that he will prioritise the Mwandi to Mulobezi road and the Simungoma to Luampa road once re-elected back into office.

President Hichilema notes that the Kazungula-Sesheke road has already been ear-marked for construction and the contractor has been engaged adding that he will soon move on site.

The Head of State expressed awareness of the dilapidated state of the road which will soon be constructed and upgraded to bituminous standard in order to improve on the business transactions along the route.

President Hichilema was speaking during a community engagement in Mwandi district of Western Province.

He has also directed that all volunteer nurses and teachers in the district be given employment immediately.

President Hichilema said the United Party for National Development (UPND) has worked more than any government before it, in providing employment for Zambians.

The Head of State cited the deployment of over 45 000 teachers, over 20 000 Nurses and doctors within 4 years 11 months.

President Hichilema said within the same period the UPND government has also employed a good number of police, Army, ZNS, ZAFF officers.

He said the UPND government deserves to be voted back in power because they have also looked at the plight of the vulnerable through the improved Social Cash Transfer, Cash for Work initiative, bursaries for secondary school and bursaries for skills training among others.

President Hichilema explained that free education has come to stay and to change the life of every vulnerable Zambian child, adding that every child has an opportunity for a better life.

“We will work on network connectivity and we want to make sure that schools are connected to ZESCO so that there’s electricity, ” he said.

President Hichilema has also revealed that once elected back into government, Mwandi district will have a fully-fledged government hospital which will employ nurses and doctors so that even medical operations can be done locally.

He has also promised the people of Mwandi a modern market.

“We will bring more boarding schools here so that the pupils won’t have to walk long distances to access schools,” he said.

President Hichilema said Mwandi is a beautiful place and needs an airstrip so that tourists and the local people can fly in and out without difficulties.

The Head of State has further called on the people in Mwandi to vote for the UPND party in the upcoming August General Elections.

He appealed to the Mwandi to vote for the UPND candidates such as Councilor, Council Chairperson, Member of Parliament and the president.

President Hichilema encouraged voters to avoid the opposition and independent candidates and only vote for UPND candidates.

World.title: Local Government showcases CDF Achievements
World.content:
The Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development says the Enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF) has significantly improved access to education, healthcare and other essential public services through infrastructure development across the country.

Speaking in an interview with the mediaat the ongoing 98th Zambia Agriculture and Commercial Show in Lusaka, Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development Principal Public Relations Officer Liseli Kanyanga, said the fund has transformed communities by financing projects that directly improve people’s lives.

Ms Kanyanga said in the education sector, government has procured more than 800,000 desks and constructed over 5,000 classroom blocks to create a conducive learning environment for pupils.

She said the initiative is in line with the Presidential directive that no child should learn while sitting on the floor and supports government’s commitment to providing quality education under the Free Education Policy.

Ms Kanyanga further said CDF has strengthened the health sector through the construction of more than 500 health posts across the country.

She added that local authorities have procured 156 ambulances, with each constituency receiving one ambulance to improve access to emergency healthcare services.

The Principal Public Relations Officer added that government has also drilled more than 6,000 boreholes in schools, health facilities and other public institutions to improve access to clean and safe water.

She noted that the ministry has further enhanced rural connectivity by enabling local authorities to procure yellow machines for road maintenance.

Ms Kanyanga said from 2022 to the first quarter of 2026, local authorities graded more than 5,000 kilometres of gravel roads, making it easier for people to access schools, health facilities and markets.

“We have done quite a number of activities, in an effort to enhance service delivery,” she noted.

She said the infrastructure projects being implemented through the Enhanced Constituency Development Fund continue to improve the quality of life for citizens and support government’s decentralisation agenda.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development Senior Solid Waste Management officer Nachombe Nang’amba highlighted how the ministry is fostering trade and investment by digitising services in local authorities to improve efficiency and ease of doing business.

Ms Nang’amba said the ministry is implementing the programme in phases across the country.

She disclosed that Lusaka and Kitwe City Councils are among the flagship local authorities that have begun offering digital services through the e-Council platform.

She explained that the platform enables citizens and businesses to pay for permits, land rates and other council services online, eliminating the need for lengthy manual processes.

Ms Nang’amba said the digitalisation of council services has significantly reduced the turnaround time for processing payments and updating levies.

She noted that the initiative is creating a more business friendly environment by improving access to public services and enhancing operational efficiency in local authorities.

“Our citizens and business houses are now able to use the digital platform under the e-Council system to pay for permits, land rates and other services,” she added.

Ms Nang’amba said the ministry remains committed to expanding the digitalisation programme to more local authorities as part of government’s efforts to foster trade, attract investment and improve service delivery across the country.

World.title: The Merits of Free Eduction in Zambia.
World.content:
THE MERITS OF FREE EDUCATION IN ZAMBIA

By Dr O’Brien Kaaba

The Zambian government, in 2021, introduced free education for primary and secondary education. In 2026, through the enactment of the Education (Amendment) Act, the government took legislative measures to turn the standard of free education into a binding legal norm. As a result, children attending childcare, primary and secondary schools in public institutions are not required to pay admission, tuition or accommodation fees. The benefits of the policy are self-evident: more than 2.5 million additional learners have been enrolled or retained in school; a huge financial burden has been lifted off the shoulders of parents; and the lives of many children are being transformed for the better by simply having an opportunity to remain in school. To support the free education policy, government has since 2022 employed more than 34,000 teachers (the highest teacher recruitment in the history of the country), more than 850,000 desks have been delivered to schools, and the government has constructed more than 3,500 new classrooms.

However, in recent weeks and months, the free education policy has been heavily criticised by some people, for various reasons, often arguing that it was prematurely implemented and should either be stopped or scaled down until available infrastructure and learning equipment is able to comfortably serve the learners. Cephas Lumina, for example, in an article published by the Mast newspaper on 16 July 2026 entitled “Free Education in Zambia: The gap between the UPND’s claims and the classroom reality” strongly criticises the free education policy, in part stating: “The UPND opened the gate quickly. But in too many places, classrooms, teachers, desks, laboratories, sanitation facilities and learning materials did not expand at the same speed.”

I argue in this article that although the free education policy may have some implementation challenges, the approach is consistent with international human rights standards and must be lauded and all efforts must be geared towards its improvement rather than its destruction.

The starting point is that education is a right. No child should be left out. Arguments implying that some children should only be allowed to access education when the infrastructure or equipment is adequate are an antithesis of the right to education and turn education into a privilege for a few instead of a universal right claimable by all. The right to education is enshrined in several international human rights treaties. Article 13(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966, for example, imposes a duty on states parties to “recognise the right of everyone to education.” The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child 1990 is more explicit about the right to education for children. Article 11(1) emphatically states that: “Every child shall have the right to education.” The phrase “every child” entails that no child should be left out. Education is not just for some children but every child. And the use of the word “shall” means education is mandatory. According to General Comment No 9 on Article 11 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child on the Right to Education (2025), the phrase “shall” “makes the right to education superlatively mandatory” and “enforces the fact that access to education is an absolute right of every child.” Because education is mandatory, states parties have an obligation to enact laws to ensure basic education is free. By enacting free education into law, the Zambian government fulfils this obligation.

Education is not only a right in itself but impacts the enjoyment of other rights. General Comment No 13 on the Right to Education (1999) recognises that “education is both a human right in itself and an indispensable means of realizing other human rights” and that education, as an empowerment right, is “the primary vehicle by which economically and socially marginalized adults and children can lift themselves out of poverty and obtain the means to participate fully in their communities.”

The merits of education as a vital mechanism for “empowering women, safeguarding children from exploitative and hazardous labour and sexual exploitation, promoting human rights and democracy, protecting the environment, and controlling population growth” are well documented. Beyond its practical value, the General Comment No 13 has noted that education is a value in itself that enhances the quality of human existence: “a well-educated, enlightened and active mind, able to wander freely and widely, is one of the joys and rewards of human existence.”

It goes without saying that the free education policy is not a magical wand that can transform the education sector overnight and wipe out all the challenges. There is still need for more teachers, for adequate classrooms, and for teaching aids and materials. As is already well known, the normative content of the right to education is availability, accessibility, acceptability and adaptability.

The enjoyment of human rights is always work in progress and there is no country that has a perfect human rights record. However, every step taken to make education a reality to all, especially the poorest and most marginalised in society, is a positive step that deserves commendation. Every step in the right direction should be celebrated and unfounded criticism that seek the destruction of making education accessible to all, however imperfect the circumstances, must be condemned as inconsistent with human rights standards. As General Comment 13 noted, retrogressive measures in relation to the right to education are impermissible. As a country, we can only seek to improve on the current system and not seek its destruction and turn education into a privilege accessible only to those with means.

(the author teaches law at the University of Zambia)

World.title: Africa: Mastercard Foundation Commits $500 Million to Transform Higher Education
World.content:
interview

Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — As Africa grapples with shrinking international development funding and rising pressure to create jobs for its rapidly growing youth population, the Mastercard Foundation is making one of the continent's biggest long-term investments in higher education, committing US$500 million over the next decade to transform African universities.

In an interview with AllAfrica's Melody Chironda, Dr. John Nkengasong, Executive Director for Higher Education, Collaboratives and Strategic Initiatives at the Mastercard Foundation, said the Foundation views universities as critical engines for developing the talent, innovation, and leadership needed to drive Africa's economic transformation. He argued that strategic investment in higher education has helped countries around the world build knowledge-based economies. He said African institutions have the potential to play the same role by preparing young people for dignified work while advancing research, entrepreneurship, and inclusive development.

Nkengasong, a Cameroonian-American virologist, was the inaugural Director of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and served as the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator in the Biden administration and the World Health Organization Special Envoy for Africa during the COVID-19 pandemic,

$500 million over a decade is a significant bet on higher education specifically, at a moment when many donors are pulling back from Africa. Why did the Foundation choose universities as the lever, rather than, say, direct scholarships or workforce programs?



Human capital investment, through higher education, is at the centre of every story of national economic transformation around the world. Through strategic investments in higher education for human capital development, many countries around the world have successfully transformed from resource-scarce nations into advanced, knowledge-based economies with sustained GDP growth. With strategic investments in higher education, Africa can generate the necessary talent that can propel the continent towards economic growth and sustained livelihoods for its young people.

The Mastercard Foundation is committed to a world where every young person has the opportunity to learn and prosper. Our Young Africa Works strategy aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the Africa Higher Education for Transformation (AHEFT) Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as a catalyst for talent development, expanded opportunities for young people, and inclusive socio-economic growth. Building on two decades of experience supporting African institutions to reimagine higher education, the AHEFT Prize converts proven success into sustained momentum through a decade-long commitment to advancing homegrown excellence and driving system-wide transformation across the continent.

The Prize talks about 'systemic, institution-wide transformation' rather than individual achievement. How do you actually measure that a university has transformed, as opposed to simply having a strong department or a few good graduates?

The AHEFT Prize is not intended to rank institutions, departments, or graduates. Instead, it aims to establish a benchmark for transformational impact in African higher education. All applications were assessed against a common set of criteria, including transformational impact, alignment with Africa's development priorities, community engagement, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration. Through their applications, African institutions are defining what transformation looks like by sharing their own stories of innovation, impact, and measurable change.

The Prize focused on institution-wide transformation rather than isolated excellence. It assessed whether change is embedded across the university's core functions, including teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment and whether that change delivers measurable outcomes for students, communities, and society.

The inaugural winners exemplified this wide-ranging transformation in different ways. From creating effective pathways from learning to earning, to advancing applied research and innovation, strengthening health systems, influencing national development priorities, and expanding regional and continental impact. Together, they demonstrate that transformational universities do more than excel in a single department; they become engines of opportunity, innovation, and socio-economic progress.

What insights did this inaugural cycle provide, and how will those lessons inform the Prize as it expands to universities across the continent?

The inaugural cycle reinforced the critical role of African higher education institutions as drivers of human capital development and socio-economic progress, showcasing diverse models of transformational impact across the continent. It also validated the importance of assessing universities holistically and in context, examining how leadership, systems, partnerships, teaching, research, and student outcomes work together to create lasting change. These insights will help strengthen future cycles of the Prize as we identify, recognize, and elevate a broader range of institutions delivering institution-wide transformation and measurable impact for young people and society.

Every winning institution has a genuinely different story, from refugee employment in Uganda to health workforce training in Rwanda. Is there a common thread the jury was really looking for, or is 'transformation' being defined differently in each context?

Every application was assessed against the same standardized criteria: transformational impact, relevance to Africa's development priorities, community engagement and service, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration and partnerships. We see this diversity as a strength.

The winning institutions demonstrated the breadth of transformational impact being driven by African higher education institutions. Across diverse contexts, they are strengthening pathways from education to employment and entrepreneurship, advancing applied research and innovation to address societal challenges, transforming health systems through workforce development and clinical excellence, and embedding industry-relevant, experiential learning. Beyond their campuses, these institutions are influencing policy, contributing to national and regional development, fostering strategic partnerships, and building resilient, sustainable models that position higher education as a catalyst for human capital development, innovation, and inclusive socio-economic growth across Africa.

How does the Foundation think about supporting these institutions to keep the momentum going after the initial $3 million grant?

Beyond the financial award, the AHEFT Prize will provide programmatic support to help winning institutions scale their transformation initiatives. We will also bring winners together to share learning, foster collaboration, and amplify their work to create ripple effects across institutions and ecosystems. The inaugural Higher Education for Transformation Convening, scheduled for September 22 in Accra, marks the beginning of this journey.

Leveraging the Foundation's network of more than 200 African higher education institutions, the goal is to create a platform through which institutions can access the support, partnerships, and connections needed to sustain and scale their transformative work.

You've committed to at least 150 institutions over ten years, but Africa has thousands of higher education institutions. How do you think about the trade-off between depth of impact at a few flagship universities versus breadth across the continent's weaker systems?

The Prize is designed to achieve both depth and scale. First, it strengthens high-performing institutions so their impact in teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment can reach more young people. Second, it seeks to catalyze broader system-wide change by demonstrating what transformative higher education can look like and encouraging governments, funders, and institutions to invest in and adopt similar approaches. This is an ambitious goal that the Foundation cannot achieve alone. We recognize that we are one of many stakeholders working toward the same objective.

Beyond the Prize itself, the Foundation advances systemic transformation through Higher Education Collaboratives- multi-stakeholder partnerships across sectors with significant potential for job creation and social impact, including health, agriculture, climate resilience, digital transformation, and education. For example, the Africa Higher Education Health Collaborative brings together universities across the continent to strengthen health workforce development and health entrepreneurship, extending impact far beyond individual institutions.

Close 

Africa's graduate unemployment and brain drain numbers remain stark. Where does this Prize actually move the needle on young people finding dignified work at home, versus simply making strong universities stronger?

Supporting universities and improving employment outcomes for young people are linked and aligned to our Young Africa Works strategy, which aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the AHEFT Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as critical human capital and talent infrastructure, enabling institutions to deliver quality, inclusive, and industry-relevant education that prepares young people for dignified and meaningful work. This is why transitions to employment is one of the Prize's four core thematic areas, alongside teaching and learning, research, and entrepreneurship.

The AHEFT Prize launches as some traditional donors are stepping back from the continent. Do you see the AHEFT Prize as the Foundation stepping into a gap left by others, and does that change how much responsibility philanthropic capital should carry for Africa's education systems?

For more than 20 years, the Mastercard Foundation has partnered with African institutions and witnessed their ability to redefine what higher education can deliver. Rather than responding to changes in the funding landscape, the AHEFT Prize builds on this experience, transforming proven success into momentum through a long-term commitment to recognize, elevate, and scale African-led excellence. By strengthening universities and the broader higher education ecosystem, the Prize aims to advance talent development, innovation, and leadership, enabling institutions across the continent to become powerful engines of opportunity and socio-economic transformation for millions of young people.

World.title: Malawi: Women Turn Cotton Profits Into Year-Round Businesses
World.content:
These Malawi Women Cotton Farmers are Turning one Harvest Into Year Round Income

A women's farming group in southern Malawi is reinvesting cotton earnings in poultry, livestock, shops and savings schemes—turning a seasonal crop into year-round income, new jobs and greater financial independence. Their progress also shows what Malawi's struggling cotton sector could deliver if persistent problems with seed, prices and market access are addressed.

As the first rays of sunlight spread across the cotton fields of Mbapi in Mangochi District, southern Malawi, Juliana Samuel walks slowly between rows of harvested plants, pointing beyond the empty stalks to a modest brick house topped with shiny iron sheets.

"Everything you see here came from cotton," she says with a smile. "I was once renting a house and struggling to provide for my children. Cotton changed my life."



For Samuel, a single mother and chairperson of the Mkuyu Women's Group, cotton is much more than a cash crop: It is the foundation upon which she has built a permanent home, started a grocery business and regained financial independence.

Her story mirrors that of 24 other women in the group, who have transformed seasonal cotton harvests into lasting economic opportunities not only for themselves but also for their wider community.

Founded in 2018, the group cultivates a shared 0.4-hectare cotton field (about 4,000 square metres), while the members also manage their own individual plots. The collective approach allows them to combine labour, share knowledge and invest their earnings in projects that benefit everyone.

According to Mkuyu group chairperson, Juliana Samuel, during the 2025/2026 farming season, the group harvested six bales of seed cotton from its communal field, earning approximately MK1.2 million (about US$670) after selling the crop.

Instead of sharing the money among the members, the group reinvested much of it into the future by repairing the group's poultry house; purchasing chicken feed, medicines, and a backpack sprayer for cotton production. Some proceeds were saved through a village savings group.

The investment builds on an earlier milestone: In 2022, after earning MK1.6 million (about US$890) from cotton sales, the women constructed the chicken house and established a poultry enterprise.

Today, the project has grown to nearly 80 laying chickens, supplying eggs and chickens to local restaurants, while providing the group with additional source of income beyond the cotton season.

"The profits from cotton don't end with cotton," Samuel explains. "We use them to build other businesses that continue bringing money throughout the year."

**Expanding income for annual support**

Those businesses have become an important buffer against the seasonal nature of cotton farming, a development experts applaud.

"Cotton farming is seasonal," explains local agricultural economist, Leonard Chimwaza. "Farmers receive income between April and June, so they need to invest in other economic activities that generate money throughout the year, effectively reducing poverty and improving household resilience through multiple streams of income."

For Samuel, every cotton harvest has marked another step forward.

After harvesting five bales from her one-acre field during the 2018/2019 season, she earned MK600, 000 (about US$335) from which she spent MK350, 000 (about US$195) on molding bricks for her first permanent home, while she used the remaining money to buy maize, Malawi's staple food, for her family.

The following season, with improved prices, Samuel earned MK950, 000 (about US$530) from her cotton sales and she started the construction of her house. The determined farmers further invested some proceeds back in cotton production materials.

But that was not all: Samuel also ordered the first stock for her small grocery business.

Her most recent harvest brought MK1 million (about US$560) and around MK700,000 (about US$390) went towards roofing of the house, while the remaining cash helped her build a permanent room that will soon become her grocery shop.

"My dream is to own a big grocery shop," Samuel says. "I believe cotton will help me achieve it."

**Knowledge that raises farmers' returns**

Across the village, 42-year-old Doreen Kasoka tells a similar story.

Before joining the Mkuyu Women Group, Kasoka had grown cotton for five years but she struggled to make meaningful profits due to lack of technical knowledge.

But everything changed after becoming part of the women's group where training in improved farming practices significantly increased her productivity, allowing her to turn cotton into a profitable business.

During the 2024/2025 season, the profits enabled her to build the house where she now lives.

"This is my house," she says proudly, pointing towards the newly built structure. "Cotton built it."

The following season proved even more rewarding for Kasoka as she earned MK2.8 million (about US$1,560) from cotton sales, and she spent part of the money in buying goats to begin livestock farming, while another portion was used to pay school fees for her children.

"Cotton has changed my life," she says. "I encourage other women to start growing it because it can remove families from poverty."

For another member, 42-year-old widow, Bessie Maliwata, the crop has brought dignity after years of hardships of providing for the family single-handedly.

"Previously, I couldn't easily pay school fees or provide for my children," she recalls, adding: "But since I joined cotton farming in 2018, life has steadily improved."

Today, Maliwata supports four children - including one in university- using income earned from cotton; and she has also invested in 15 chickens and 12 goats, creating additional income streams that strengthen her household's resilience against future shocks.

**Investing beyond the cotton field**

Similar success stories are also reflected broadly in parts of Malawi's cotton-growing areas, including Neno, another southern region district where organised farmer groups are treating cotton as a business by following recommended farming practices, and investing their profits into new enterprises.

Grace Mbekeyani, an agricultural extension officer working under African Institute of Corporate Citizenship (AICC), acknowledges how women are increasingly using cotton income beyond meeting immediate household needs.

"Cotton is no longer simply a cash crop for many women," she says. "It has become a pathway to education, entrepreneurship and financial independence as the women establish businesses such as poultry production, grocery shops, irrigation farming, tailoring and soap making."

The AICC's Women's Economic Empowerment in the Cotton Value Chain project, implemented with support from We Effect and the Embassy of Sweden, has strengthened this transition by training thousands of smallholder farmers in financial literacy, climate-smart agriculture and business development.

The initiative supports 2,400 cotton farmers in the area alone, while around 2,200 participate in Village Savings and Loan Associations that help them save, borrow and invest in productive enterprises.

**A sector operating below its potential**

Beyond improving the group members' household incomes, the cotton benefits extend to the wider rural economy through seasonal employment, as evidenced by 48-year-old family man, Leonard Gray, who is among five workers for the women's Group.

"The money I earn here helps me support my family," he says. "It also helps me invest in my own cotton farming, and pay school fees for my children.

But while the stories of Samuel, Kasoka and Maliwata demonstrate cotton's transformative potential, challenges such as access to markets; low prices; delayed delivery of seed; poor germination rates; and increasing pest infestations continue to threaten the sector

According to the Mkuyu Women's Group, the nearest cotton buying depot is about 11 kilometers away, attracting MK10, 000 (about US$6) in transport to deliver their produce.

On pricing, the farmers say they had expected an offer of at least MK2,000 per kilogram (about US$1.10) during the 2025/2026 marketing season but they were only offered MK1,500 per kilogram (about US$0.84).

Authorities acknowledge the prevailing challenges farmers face and offer hope, saying banks, cotton companies and seed regulators are working together to improve investment in the sector.

"Delayed delivery of seed often forces farmers to plant outside the recommended window, reducing yields," agricultural extension officer, Mbekeyani, explains, adding: "Poor-quality seed, pests and diseases continue to affect production, while climate change is increasing pressure on farmers."

Close 

The poor access to quality seed has led to years of declining output, with annual cotton production averaging only about 10,000 metric tonnes over the past five years, leaving many ginneries operating below capacity while reducing economic opportunities across rural communities.

**Putting Malawi's cotton sector on the path to recovery**

"The sector is in recovery mode," says Cotton Council of Malawi Public Relations Officer, Prisca Jamali. "Around 30,000 farming households currently grow cotton in Malawi, despite the country's potential to support more than 200,000 cotton-producing families."

According to the Cotton Council, if Malawi were to produce 45,000 metric tonnes of cotton, the sector could generate approximately MWK95.5 billion (about US$53 million) in foreign exchange; MWK74.3 billion (about US$41 million) in farm income; with around 18,000 post-harvest jobs created, excluding employment generated on farms.

Besides underproduction, lack of value addition is another challenge that is generally affecting cotton industry in Malawi, with approximately 95 percent of the country's cotton being exported as lint, meaning much of the value addition takes place outside the country, says Jamali.

As the country strives to put the cotton sector fully on track, for Juliana Samuel the evidence of the crop's value stands just a few metres from the field where she continues to plant every season.

Standing outside the brick shop she is gradually completing with proceeds from cotton, she reflects on a journey that began with a rented house and a little more determination.

"Ndipitiliza kulima Thonje, nyengo yaulimiwu ikafika ndikumasendera chifupi ndi loto langa. Thonje lasintha moyo wanga," said Samuel in Chichewa, which means: "I will continue growing cotton, every season brings me closer to my dream, cotton has transformed my life".

For the women of Mkuyu Group in general, cotton is no longer simply harvested and sold: It is being transformed into businesses, employment and hope.

World.title: Africa: Cotton Farmers Could Earn From Soil Carbon Credits
World.content:
A scheme tested in Uzbekistan could let African cotton farmers earn twice over, once for the fibre and once for the carbon stored in the soil beneath their fields.

Cotton has always paid farmers for what they harvest. Its next payout may come from what stays in the soil, as carbon held on African farms could soon become a tradeable asset.

Farmers who qualify could earn up to $200 a hectare on top of whatever the crop itself fetches, a sum that in parts of West Africa can rival the harvest income it sits on.

The bid comes from the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC), a Washington body that coordinates cotton policy across producing and buying nations.



On April 30th it announced a plan to pay growers for carbon rather than fibre, provided they change how they farm. That means planting cover crops, cutting back on ploughing, and working biochar into their fields.

Biochar is charred organic matter, plant waste burned under controlled conditions until it stops breaking down easily. Worked into soil, it holds water and carbon in place for years. Paired with less ploughing, which normally exposes buried carbon to the air and lets it escape, the combination keeps more carbon underground than conventional farming does.

The proposed model would convert cotton stalks and other eligible agricultural residues into biochar and compost, which would then be returned to agricultural soils.

Dr Keshav Kranthi, the committee's chief scientist, explained that "biochar improves soil structure, stores water and nutrients and promotes microbial growth. It is a sustainable solution that has a positive impact on both the environment and the profitability of agriculture."

But ICAC stresses that the initiative is "first and foremost a soil-health and regenerative-agriculture program." Its Director of Communications, Mike McCue, told bird story agency that "carbon finance is intended to make those improvements affordable and sustainable for cotton farmers over the long term."

The advisory framed this as a change that pays farmers on two fronts at once, techniques its Executive Director Eric Trachtenberg describes as within every farmer's reach.

"With simple techniques, cotton farmers can improve the quality of their soil and at the same time sequester carbon in the soil for more than 100 years," he said.

That buried carbon is what the advisory intends to sell. Already, firms worldwide buy credits each year to offset emissions they cannot cut directly, and a tonne of carbon kept underground is worth money to them regardless of whose field it sits under.

Foresters have been trading carbon for years. In June last year, the World Bank Group said the DRC earned $19.47 million for reducing 3.89 million tonnes of emissions in MaiâNdombe — the first instalment of a deal worth up to $55 million for cutting 11 million tonnes.

"A significant share of the funds will go to local communities and Indigenous peoples who are helping lead forest conservation efforts on the ground," the lender said.

Cotton, meanwhile, a crop better known for depleting soil than restoring it, has not raked in such carbon-based earnings for farmers.

But selling that carbon means proving it exists, and proof is where earlier schemes stumbled. Audits of several forest protection projects found credits issued for carbon that was never actually saved, in some cases for trees that were never at risk of being cut down.

Airlines and consumer companies that bought those credits ended up holding paper that offset far less than claimed. The wider market has not fully recovered its credibility since.

The committee has handed that problem to Merago, a carbon market firm hired to track soil conditions on participating farms, check results against international standards, and manage credit sales once certified.

"The initiative is currently in the preparatory stage," McCue explained. "We are discussing potential projects with implementing agencies in member countries."

The next steps will register farmers, gather baseline soil information and work out how much biomass each area can supply.

They will then train local personnel, set up digital monitoring and send each project for independent validation under a recognised carbon standard.

That has prompted the committee to hold back on any timetable for issuing or selling credits until removals are properly documented, verified and certified. Early estimates suggest two to three credits a hectare each year, shaped by local conditions and the standard applied.

From there, Uzbekistan emerged as the natural starting point. Its cotton grows mostly on large, stateâorganised farms, a structure that allows wide areas to be checked quickly and cheaply.

Africa, on the other hand, is the harder test. GIZ, Germany's development agency, puts the continent's share of global raw cotton exports at about 10% to 15%, with some four million households – encompassing roughly 20 million people – growing the crop, most on a hectare or two rather than the sprawling plots common in Uzbekistan.

Benin, Burkina Faso, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire rank among the world's larger producers, and in each the crop is grown mainly by smallholders lacking the scale that made the Uzbek pilot simple to monitor.

Checking soil carbon across thousands of small, scattered plots costs more per tonne than checking a handful of large ones. Someone has to group scattered farmers together to interest a buyer, and someone has to pay for testing before any credit is sold, since farmers themselves rarely have the cash to front it. The committee has not yet said who does either job.

Kranthi has pointed to this structural gap when discussing cotton sustainability schemes more broadly. Such verification, he says, "can be challenging in Asia and Africa because the crop is primarily grown by smallholder farmers," who account for more than 90% of global cotton production.

For the Aid by Trade Foundation (AbTF), whose Cotton made in Africa (CmiA) standard already covers about 36% of African cotton production, the groundwork for such a transition is already being laid.

Holger Diedrich, the foundation's project manager for communications, said that "farmers that are part of the Cotton made in Africa initiative already adhere to principles that reduce environmental impact and improve the quality of the soil."

"These practices inherently contribute to carbon sequestration or emission reduction, making the transition to generating carbon credits more straightforward. They are already doing much of the groundwork." Farmers, he added, can also benefit from a reduction or complete replacement of expensive fertilisers with biochar.

One thing favours African growers regardless, because soil farmed hard for years, as much of the continent's cotton land has been, generally has more room to absorb new carbon than soil already well managed.

Land run down the most often has the most to gain, and gain is what the carbon market pays for. Under the right conditions it can take up carbon faster in its first seasons of recovery than land that was never depleted at all.

Close 

Asked about barriers to participation, the foundation stayed focused on the upside. "This initiative has the potential to be an ecological and economic game changer that radiates far beyond Africa," Diedrich said.

"It could finally reward small-scale cotton farmers south of the Sahara for what they achieve every day." Diedrich declined to offer advice for other markets weighing similar schemes, calling it premature this early on.

McCue also cautioned, saying the programme should not be sold as quick cash for farmers.

“Our aim is not to promote carbon credits as a quick or guaranteed payment,” he said, adding that the goal is a transparent system where carbon revenues support biochar production, composting, training and monitoring, with benefits shared under an accountable framework. ICAC's main role, he said, will be to provide the technical knowledge, training and scientific support required to implement the program responsibly.

Whether that potential reaches an actual farmer depends on decisions the committee has not made public. The $200 figure is a ceiling reached under strong conditions, not a typical result, and its invitation for governments, companies and certification bodies to help fund the next phase suggests it cannot scale the programme alone.

What Uzbekistan has shown is that cotton can create a new revenue line when farmers rebuild their soil. Whether that revenue reaches a smallholder in Benin as reliably as it reaches a state farm in Uzbekistan is what the next phase will reveal.

World.title: East Africa: American Analyst Warns Eritrea's Proxy Strategy Risks Destabilizing Horn of Africa
World.content:
Addis Ababa — American geopolitical analyst Andrew Korybko has warned that the Eritrean regime's proxy strategy could further destabilize the Horn of Africa, fuel insecurity and threaten regional stability.

In his recent article, "Eritrea's Hybrid War on Ethiopia Threatens To Set The Whole Horn Ablaze," Korybko contends that Eritrea's policies under Isaias Afwerki are driven by a strategic objective of preventing Ethiopia from emerging as a strong regional power.

Drawing on recent developments, the analyst argues that Eritrea's strategy has included alleged support for anti-peace armed groups, contributing to the persistence of conflicts and instability across the Horn of Africa.



Korybko's assessment aligns with observations made by Getachew Reda, Adviser to Prime Minister on East African Affairs, during the Ethiopian National Defense College's Annual National Security Conference held in late June.

Getachew underscored that Eritrea's strategic calculations are based on ensuring that Ethiopia remains politically and economically weakened.

"Eritrea conceptualizes its security as being ensured by a weak Ethiopia," Korybko wrote.

He characterized Eritrea's actions as a form of hybrid warfare, combining political pressure, covert support for insurgent groups, and efforts to hinder Ethiopia's economic progress and national cohesion.

The analyst further argued that Addis Ababa has repeatedly proposed expanding economic cooperation with Eritrea--including reported offers involving strategic investments and infrastructure partnerships linked to reliable and unrestricted access to the sea.

However, these initiatives were rejected by Asmara, the America analyst stated.

According to Korybko, closer economic integration would not only strengthen Ethiopia's economy but also accelerate regional development, making such cooperation strategically undesirable from Eritrea's perspective.

He noted that Ethiopian advocates a dual-track response centered on accelerating national development and infrastructure projects while intensifying diplomatic efforts to secure sea access and strengthen regional cooperation.

Korybko also argued that the Horn of Africa's security landscape has become increasingly complex due to Egypt's strategic alignment with Eritrea.

He claimed that Cairo is using Eritrea as a proxy to contain Ethiopia, transforming longstanding bilateral disputes into a broader geopolitical challenge with implications for the entire region.

"The real threat to regional peace comes from Egypt, but the most direct one comes from Eritrea," Korybko wrote, warning that the Horn of Africa risks becoming another theater of proxy competition with potentially far-reaching consequences.

Close 

Drawing parallels with geopolitical rivalries in other regions, the analyst cautioned that continued tensions could heighten the risk of wider conflict unless addressed through sustained diplomacy, regional dialogue, and confidence-building measures.

Korybko concluded that Ethiopia should continue strengthening its economic resilience, national development, and diplomatic engagement while remaining vigilant to evolving regional security challenges.

He further warned that unless Eritrea changes its current course or the international community takes more decisive steps to encourage de-escalation, the Horn of Africa's fragile peace could come under increasing strain, with consequences extending well beyond the region.

World.title: Nigeria: Tinubu Told to Nominate Jonathan for UN Secretary-General
World.content:
Yenagoa — The African Policy and Research Consortium (APRC) has called on President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to nominate former President Goodluck Jonathan for the position of United Nations Secretary-General.

In a statement on Thursday, the convener of APRC, Prof. Edward Agbai, said Jonathan possessed the leadership experience, diplomatic skills and democratic credentials required to occupy the world's top diplomatic position.

Agbai said the UN needed a leader with proven executive experience and the ability to navigate complex global challenges.

"The United Nations needs a leader with proven executive experience, democratic credentials, and the ability to manage complex global challenges," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The group highlighted Jonathan's political experience as Nigeria's Vice-President from 2007 to 2010 and President from 2010 to 2015, describing his leadership record as evidence of his capacity for responsible governance.

APRC also praised Jonathan's decision to concede defeat after the 2015 presidential election, describing it as a significant contribution to democratic development in Africa.

According to the group, the peaceful transfer of power strengthened Nigeria's democracy and demonstrated Jonathan's commitment to constitutional order and national stability.

The consortium noted that since leaving office, Jonathan had continued to support democracy, peacebuilding and conflict resolution efforts across Africa through election observation and mediation assignments under organisations including the African Union, ECOWAS, COMESA, IGAD and the West African Elders Forum.

APRC said Jonathan's approach of dialogue, consultation and consensus-building had earned him international recognition, adding that such qualities were essential for a UN Secretary-General saddled with the responsibility of mediating conflicts and promoting global cooperation.

The group further argued that Jonathan's experience leading Nigeria's diverse population gives him a strong understanding of global development, security and environmental challenges.

It added that the emergence of an African candidate for the position would strengthen the continent's voice and influence in global governance.

APRC urged the Federal Government to begin diplomatic engagements with African countries and other international partners to build support for Jonathan's candidacy.

While acknowledging that securing the position requires broad international backing, the consortium said every successful campaign begins with identifying a credible candidate.

The group maintained that Jonathan's record of democratic leadership, regional diplomacy and peaceful conflict resolution makes him a strong contender for the UN Secretary-General role.

Close 

It urged President Tinubu to support Jonathan's nomination, saying the move would advance Nigeria's diplomatic interests and promote Africa's push for greater representation in global institutions.

World.title: Liberia: Police Say Their Own Officers Escorted the Cocaine, Charge Two Commanders
World.content:
Serving Liberian police commanders drove escort for the country's largest cocaine consignment as it was moved from the shoreline where it came ashore to the stash house where it was later seized, and two of them were charged and sent to court Thursday, Inspector General of Police Gregory Coleman said.

It is the first time the state has accused officers of moving the narcotics themselves rather than of interfering with the investigation after the fact, and it puts the police at the center of the trafficking operation they are investigating.

"We have identified key state actors who played a role in transporting, escorting the movement of these narcotic substance from the landing site to the holding ground using police vehicles as escort, one in the front, one in the back," Coleman said at the Ministry of Information's regular press briefing.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He named the chief of highway patrol, Wadell Quaboe and the chief of major crimes Anthony Blaye, both of whom were detained at Police Headquarters and, he said, would be turned over to court the same day for prosecution. A deputy commander at Roberts International Airport for the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency has also been identified as a key actor, Coleman said, and other state actors remain under investigation.

"The investigation continues with them," he said. "When the time is right, we will be putting the information out."

Coleman said investigators have established that the shipment could not have entered the country without official protection. "One key thing that you all should know is that these traffickers would never be brave to enter our country with this particular extent of narcotic substances," he said. "They had assistance."

He went considerably further than the police have gone before on who provided it, telling reporters the operation was authorized at the top of a previous government. The investigation has reached 2021, he said, and is examining people who held presidential appointments between 2019 and 2023.

"This thing was definitively sanctioned by state actors at very, very senior level," Coleman said.

He did not name anyone at that level, produce documents, or say whether any of those former officials have been questioned.

The seizure was not a lucky interception, according to Coleman, but the end of a surveillance operation that ran more than a year, led by the National Security Agency with the Executive Protection Service and the police joining later, and authorized for takedown by the National Security Council. He said an earlier attempt to bring the drugs in by air failed, after which the traffickers switched to a sea route.

Coleman framed the case as the return of an industry Liberia had once driven out. He said a United States Drug Enforcement Administration special operations mission requested by then President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf ran from 2008 to 2013, that 11 people connected to cartel operations were expelled to the Southern District of New York, and that all were convicted and sentenced to between five and 33 years. Cartels stayed away until roughly 2018, he said, and returned about two years into the current administration on the belief that the networks that once protected them could be reactivated.

Foreign assistance has since been secured at the president's request, Coleman said. "The DEA is currently in-country working alongside us. We have agents, we have analysts here working along with us on this investigation." Morocco has responded to a request for support, he said, and he spoke Thursday with the inspector general of the Rwanda National Police about sending a team.

Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Oswald Tweh, who heads the joint investigative team, said cooperation had also been sought from the Netherlands. He said he and the national security adviser met the Dutch justice and security minister in Accra on July 21, and that he and the officer in charge of the LDEA had met Dutch officials in Accra in November on the margins of a conference on West African drug markets convened with the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

Asked directly whether the investigation had been blocked from questioning Joseph Nyuma Boakai Jr., the president's son, whose name has circulated in connection with the case, Cllr. Tweh said no one is exempt.

"There will be no limits," he said. "We will not jump on people because the crowd out there is yelling. Everything will be evidence-based."

"If the evidence leads to you, you'll be investigated," Tweh said.

Coleman said the same, and declined to go further. "At any point in time when the need comes up, you will hear from us," he said.

On the money, Coleman gave a figure far below what has circulated publicly. He said the raid was accompanied by a court sheriff, that the returns are on file with the court, and that the cash recovered was inside the suitcases with the drugs.

"The cash that I remember that was seized there was 7,000 US dollars," he said.

Coleman also accused unnamed people in the media of taking cartel money, saying the traffickers have effectively unlimited resources. "We've been able to verify and establish that they have infused money into the media to change the narrative, distract the key players in the investigation, and just sow a serious seed of discord," he said.

The Ministry of Information clarified that within minutes, telling reporters that the inspector general was referring to elements within the media community, some of which operate platforms that are not Liberian entities, and that "he was not suggesting that the Liberian media collectively is receiving money from the drug cartel." Coleman accepted the clarification. "I 100 percent agree with what the minister said because that was my intent," he said.

Close 

He offered no evidence for the allegation and named no outlet or individual.

Coleman refused to specify the number of suspects, mentioning that two more had been brought in while he was on his way to the briefing. "Every hour we're finding new suspects," he said. He described the case as a multi-layered conspiracy and claimed that police are intentionally withholding details to protect a prosecution, referencing the collapse of an earlier case.

"You saw what happened here to the $100 million drug case. You saw how people walked away from the court," he said. "We don't want to make that mistake again."

The seized narcotics were being transported to a burn site Thursday under a court order, with representatives of the Environmental Protection Agency present and samples retained as evidence, Coleman said.

He also addressed the video of masked men that circulated after the seizure, dismissing it as staged.

Coleman, who has also faced allegations from opposition figures, said he still has the president's support. "The confidence of the people, the confidence of the appointing power remained, and the instructions were clear," he stated.

"So to those of you who know yourselves and you know the roles that you've played, we're on you," he said.
