World.title: Football and politics, brought to you by Big Business (and energy drinks)
World.content:
In “United Passions” — which really should have been called “Balls” — Blatter is played by Tim Roth, a fine actor who admitted he took the role to pay for his kids to go to college. If the movie was, heaven help us, ever updated to include Infantino’s tenure, surely the role would go to either Stanley Tucci or the ghost of late Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Infantino has, you will doubtless be aware, decided to sell football off to the highest bidder, with FIFA publishing a proposal that would privatize the World Cup’s commercial operations. A venture capital firm headed by Josh Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is lined up as the lead investor in the proposed deal. Of course it is. The scheme is known as FIFA Forward Enterprise or FFE — although FFS seems rather more appropriate.

I, for one, am looking forward to the Raytheon World Cup of 2038 in South Sudan, where the 18-karat gold trophy depicting two human figures holding up the Earth is replaced by a cheap plastic bobblehead of Trump with his pants around his ankles.

But not everyone is so keen on Infantino’s plan. Glenn Micallef, the EU’s sports commissioner, pointed out that football “isn’t baseball,” which is very perceptive of him. It’s also not cross-country skiing, knitting or a cauliflower.

Micallef’s point is, of course, that football hasn’t — and shouldn’t — reach the level of commercialization of American sports, although it had a damn good go during this summer’s World Cup with the introduction of hydration breaks sponsored by Powerade.

But the further monetization of sports feels inevitable; it is entertainment, after all. Will politics go the same way? When, for example, will we see EU summits sponsored by Red Bull, the European Commission midday briefing brought to you by Xanax, or Germany sponsored by sausages in a glass jar?

World.title: Why Andy Burnham is no ordinary Labour prime minister
World.content:
The Labour Party and the Co-operative Party are distinct organizations — but a pact agreed in 1927 allows candidates to stand on behalf of both parties.

In practice, Co-operative MPs tend to follow the Labour line — but the party has a distinct focus on mutual ownership, community businesses, and credit unions. It argues for democratic control of services and businesses by the people who use them — and supporters say this program offers up real hints about how Burnham will now govern.

Since returning to the Westminster frontline, the new prime minister has hardly been shy about his administration’s support for the co-operative drive.

“If people, in 1844, could form the co-operative movement in Rochdale to lower the price of food, then why can’t we act now, with similar courage, to make life better?” he asked in his first major speech after winning the Makerfield by-election. That was a direct callback to a group of working-class weavers — known as the Rochdale Pioneers — credited with founding the modern cooperative movement by pooling wages to set up a worker-owned store at a time of soaring food costs.

The Co-operative Party was “created for a slightly different purpose” to Labour, says International Development Minister Kirsty McNeill — a Labour and Co-operative MP like Burnham, It is about getting a better deal “as a consumer in the marketplace and where you live.”

“It’s going to be a moment of unprecedented opportunity for the co-operative movement,” says Caitlin Prowle, the party’s assistant general secretary. “I believe that this new team is very serious about rewiring our economy, rewiring society and shifting power.”

World.title: Russia’s Olympic win comes with a price for Putin
World.content:
But while Russia has been trumpeting its big diplomatic win, and the IOC has drawn international ire for its decision, what Moscow quietly agreed to in order to achieve its victory garnered far less attention — a quiet renunciation of what Moscow claims as “sovereign territory.”

What lies behind the IOC’s reversal was confirmation that the Russian Olympic Committee “no longer includes as its members any regional sports organisations in territories falling under the jurisdiction of the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine” — that means Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.

A woman holds a sign with the text “Boycott Russian sport at the Olympics” during a march in memory of the hundreds of Ukrainian athletes killed since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in Paris on July 13, 2024. | Remon Haazen/Getty Images

These four territories of great economic, industrial and historic importance for President Putin have been a major sticking point in ending the war since Russia annexed them in 2022 in defiance of international law. And this concession made on the global stage is now turning into a domestic political scandal, drawing criticism from the country’s influential pro-war commentators who see it as a betrayal of the Kremlin’s territorial claims.

“The Russian Olympic Committee gave up part of the country’s territory just to live it up in style at the Olympics,” wrote famous pro-war journalist Dmitry Steshin — just one of many discontented voices.

‘Sabotage at a state level’

This is not the first clash between the Kremlin’s international sports ambitions and its influential military bloggers.

Russia’s attempts to send its athletes to the 2024 Olympics under neutral status — a restriction imposed by the IOC after 2023 — had similarly triggered widespread backlash, with the country’s pro-war commentators accusing authorities of “betraying national interests.”

World.title: Italy and Spain clash over Schengen as Ceuta migration spat boils over
World.content:
“We are prepared to take action — including through extraordinary measures — to defend our borders and ensure citizens’ safety,” she added.

Meloni, along with Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani — the most senior ministers from each of the parties in Italy’s ruling right-wing coalition — has called for the suspension of the Schengen agreement, or for Spain to be kicked out of the free-travel zone.

Under the agreement, people can move freely between the 29 European signatory countries. However, several countries have reintroduced checks on some of their borders, which is allowed under the treaty, citing migration risks. Italy has already temporarily reinstituted checks on the Slovenian border to clamp down on smuggling and terrorism.

A frame grab from an AFP video showing migrants reaching the shore of the Spanish north African exclave of Ceuta after swimming around the border fence between Morocco and Spain on July 30, 2026. | Lucía Diaz/AFP via Getty Images

Tajani went further than just calling for Spain to be shut out of Schengen, pinning the blame for the Ceuta unrest on Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s migration policy — which promises to legalize hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants — calling it “profoundly wrong” and claiming it “provides and incentive for human trafficking.”

That drew a stern rebuke from Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares, who has summoned the Italian ambassador — a mark of serious diplomatic displeasure — to answer for Tajani’s comments.

“This message is unbecoming of the foreign minister of a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity, not partisan demagoguery,” he fired back in a public reply to Tajani on X.

World.title: Climate change made Spanish wildfires 20 times more likely
World.content:
The scientists had already found that climate change increased the likelihood of the record-breaking Western European heat wave in late June as well as the spring drought — both events that made land more fire-prone.

“These mega-fires show how fast climate-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into devastating national disasters,” said United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell in a statement responding to the findings.

“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is baking our planet, making these conditions more dangerous, and these megafires more deadly and destructive,” he added, calling for a faster transition from polluting fossil fuels to clean energy.

The researchers looked at a fire risk metric incorporating hot, dry and windy conditions, as well as landscape conditions during the worst fire week near Madrid and Bordeaux. They then compared this year’s situation to the worst conditions in previous summers and juxtaposed the current climate with a simulation of the planet’s pre-industrial state.

The study also established that in today’s climate, similar fire weather is expected to occur every 20 years in southwestern France and every six years in central Spain.

A key driver of the increased fire risk was weather whiplash earlier this year, with a dry spring following a wet winter, the scientists added. These conditions fueled excessive vegetation growth that then dried up, providing plenty of fuel for fires to spread.

“What we’re seeing in France and Spain isn’t just bad luck, it is a clear sign of the escalating impacts of anthropogenic warming,” said Clair Barnes, a climate scientist at Imperial College London and the lead researcher on the analysis.

"Every fraction of a degree of warming pushes us into unknown territory, and these fires show exactly what that risk looks like," she added.

World.title: UK announces £8 billion investment in nuclear submarines
World.content:
The United Kingdom has announced it plans it invest £8.4 billion (€9.8 billion) for the next phase of its Dreadnought Class nuclear submarine programme.

 

"A major £8.4bn investment in the UK's nuclear deterrent, delivering jobs and opportunity for young people for years to come," Prime Minister Andy Burnham's office said in a press release.

UK defence contractor BAE Systems is set to receive £5.9 billion (€6.9 billion) with the remaining going to the wider supply chain.

BAE Systems is taking decades of flight controls expertise underwater on-board the UK’s next generation submarine, Dreadnought. AP Photo/BAE Systems

BAE Systems has been tasked with delivering four Dreadnought Class nuclear-powered submarines as part of Britain's nuclear deterrent.

The investment was set to help the first of four submarines, the HMS Dreadnought, complete its sea trials and "be ready to enter service with the Royal Navy in the early 2030s", Downing Street said.

Burnham's government said the programme would support 47,000 jobs and apprenticeships over the next decade.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting visit Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge at BAE Systems, in England, July 30, 2026. Christopher Furlong/Pool Photo via AP

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the investment "secures our commitment to deliver Dreadnought Class submarines by backing British industry".

The UK government has earmarked more than £63 billion over the next four years to fund its nuclear deterrent as part of its Defence Investment Plan.

That includes the Dreadnought submarines and new attack submarines part of its AUKUS military alliance with Australia and the United States.

World.title: Apple shares fall despite record revenue as outlook disappoints
World.content:
Apple beat market expectations with its latest quarterly results on Thursday, thanks to strong sales of iPhones and Mac computers, capping Tim Cook's final earnings report as CEO.

 

However, investors focused on Apple’s weaker-than-expected outlook and warnings about supply constraints. The company forecast revenue growth of between 9% and 11% in the current quarter, below analysts’ expectations of around 12%.

The strong quarter was also clouded by rising memory-chip costs and shortages of advanced chipmaking capacity, partly linked to the artificial intelligence boom.

Apple previously described the surge in demand as an “unprecedented challenge” for the consumer electronics industry.

As a result, Apple announced last month that it would raise prices for some Mac and iPad models. It has not yet increased iPhone prices, although analysts expect it could do so later this year.

The maker of the iPhone and iPad said on Thursday that it earned $29.79bn (€25.9bn), or $2.02 per share, during the April-to-June period. That was up 27% from $23.43bn (€20.4bn), or $1.57 per share, a year earlier.

Revenue grew 16% to $109.42bn (€95.2bn) from $94.04bn (€81.8bn).

Revenue from iPhone sales rose by 21.7% to a quarterly record of $54.25bn (€47.2bn), while Mac revenue climbed by 28.7% to $10.35bn (€9bn).

Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.89 per share on revenue of around $109bn (€94.8bn), according to a FactSet poll. Tariff refunds contributed $0.11 per share to Apple’s earnings.

"Today, Apple is proud to report our strongest June quarter ever, with double-digit revenue growth across iPhone, Mac and Services, and in every geographic segment," said Tim Cook, Apple's CEO.

It was Cook's final earnings call before he steps down as chief executive after 15 years. John Ternus, Apple's head of hardware engineering, will take over on 1 September.

"I couldn't be more confident in his leadership, in the executive team and the extraordinary people at Apple," Cook said.

Apple continues to generate cash without the massive artificial intelligence spending facing its Big Tech peers, “and that showed across most parts of the operation,” said Thomas Monteiro, an analyst at Investing.com.

“As the market grows more worried about free cash flow trajectories elsewhere in Big Tech, Apple keeps standing out as the safe haven in the storm.”

But he cautioned that rising memory costs could challenge Apple in the coming quarters.

Cook described the surge in memory prices as a “100-year flood”, saying Apple expected its memory costs to rise further during the current quarter.

The company will also no longer benefit from the tariff refunds that boosted its latest profit margin. September’s iPhone launch and potential further price increases should “help cushion the hit”, Monteiro said.

Shares in Apple fell by as much as 8% in after-hours trading on Thursday before recovering some of those losses.

The company recently regained its position as the world's most valuable listed company from Nvidia.

World.title: Hamas agrees to 'historic' disarmament deal that includes Israeli withdrawal from Gaza
World.content:
Hamas said on Friday that it has agreed to a deal to end the war with Israel that included provisions addressing its de-weaponisation and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.

 

Earlier, US President Donald Trump announced that the so-called Board of Peace has reached what he hailed as a “historic deal” on Thursday to disarm the Gaza-based group and all other armed groups and Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza, but questions remained over conditions and timeline.

The deal, described by Trump in a post on Truth Social as a “monumental step”, comes nine months after a US-brokered ceasefire was signed to end Israel’s two year offensive on the enclave, signed in October last year in Egypt’s Sharm el Sheikh.

US President Donald Trump announces Board of Peace deal to disarm Hamas and Israel to withdraw forces from Gaza in a post on Truth Social, 31 July, 2026 @realDonaldTrump/TruthSocial

“This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people,” wrote Trump.

“At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks.”

Negotiations between Israel and Hamas had largely deadlocked over the implementation of its second phase, including the disarmament of Hamas and the reconstruction of Gaza.

President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, in Washington, Wednesday, July 29, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The US president says the deal will put to action the implementation of his 20-point peace plan in “carefully structured phases”.

Trump’s 20-point ceasefire plan calls on the Gaza-based group to surrender its weapons and destroy its vast network of tunnels. It also envisions the arrival of a new technocratic Palestinian government, led by former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, who will lead Gaza’s rebuilding efforts.

Once disarmament is complete, Trump said Israel will then withdraw its forces out of the territory and hand over policing duties to a new “International Stabilisation Force”, which will work alongside Palestinian police to safekeep Gaza.

Smoke rises following an Israeli military strike in Gaza City, Tuesday, July 28, 2026 Jehad Alshrafi/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Rumoured timeline

US and Board of Peace officials, describing the deal to reporters on condition of anonymity under guidelines set by the White House, gave an extremely optimistic assessment of the agreement.

The officials were unable to offer specific timelines for the disarmament of Hamas or other groups that operate in Gaza, such as Palestinian Islamic Jihad, but said the Gaza police force would turn over weapons to the technocratic Board of Peace-backed Gaza administration in the next two weeks.

The Gaza police force, however, does not include the vast majority of Hamas militants and heavy weaponry is not included in that part of the agreement, according to the officials.

Instead, the surrender of heavy weapons and the decommissioning of Hamas tunnels and other infrastructure are to come later in a process that could take between 200 and 350 days, a Board of Peace official said.

Israel remains sceptical

A US official said Israel, which has been deeply sceptical about Hamas’ willingness to give up its guns or relinquish at least behind-the-scenes control of Gaza, had been consulted at every step of the negotiation.

However, the official said Israel was not being asked to do anything more than what it had initially committed to when it agreed to Trump’s 20-point plan, which essentially involves withdrawing its forces from Gaza and committing to ending airstrikes on the territory.

Palestinians salvage their belongings from the rubble of a building and tents destroyed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City, Thursday, July 30, 2026 Jehad Alshrafi/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The official added that Trump would be “very, very disappointed” if Israel didn't adhere to the agreement.

The US president reiterated in his post on social media that not allowing Hamas to possess the strength it once did to pose a threat to Israel, remains a central part of the deal, adding that the new government will work to represent and serve its people.

Israel’s war on Gaza, which started in response to Hamas’ 7 October, 2023 incursion into southern Israel, killed at least 73,000 Palestinians, according to medical sources in the territory, including those killed since the ceasefire, Gaza’s Health Ministry said.

Displaced Palestinian children lineup to receive donated food at a community kitchen in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, Thursday, July 23, 2026 Abdel Kareem Hana/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met at the White House on Tuesday, but neither said much about what was discussed in their first face-to-face meeting since jointly launching the war against Iran.

Hamas announced earlier this month that it had dissolved its government in the enclave and was preparing to transfer power to a technical committee backed by the United Nations as part of the ceasefire deal.

The Israeli Defence Forces currently control more than half of Gaza, leaving Palestinians confined to squalid tent camps and heavily damaged urban neighbourhoods. The UN has repeatedly warned of dire living conditions across Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect.

World.title: Spanish invisible shield that saves satellites from irreparable failure
World.content:
The multipactor effect has been on the European Space Agency's (ESA) list of concerns for more than 40 years. It is an avalanche of electrons that occurs in vacuum, inside components such as antennas or waveguides, and can ultimately cause irreversible damage to equipment.

 

For decades, the standard solution has been to coat these parts with Alodine, a chromium-based compound that offers good protection but is harmful to the health of those who handle it and to the environment. European authorities have long been pushing for its ban, although none of the alternatives proposed so far has managed to match its technical performance.

Lidia Martínez, a CSIC researcher at the Institute of Materials Science of Madrid (source in Spanish) (ICMM), explains that the sector needed a substitute that would emit few secondary electrons, as these are what trigger the chain reaction.

Most previous attempts had focused on modifying the surface of materials at the micrometre scale, without achieving the leap in performance demanded by the space industry.

Nanoparticle generation system to prevent the multipactor effect Science Direct

In this case, size really does matter, and not just the material

The ICMM team decided to change scale. Instead of working with micrometric structures, it has developed a rough surface at the nanometric level, that is, with features on the order of a billionth of a metre. To do so, they produced gold and silver nanoparticles between four and eight nanometres in size using an ultra-high-vacuum technique known as a gas aggregation source, which allows the materials to be deposited without solvents or residues.

The result is porous, metallic, chemically clean films which, according to tests carried out in ESA-accredited laboratories, reduce secondary electron emission by around 30% compared with Alodine.

In addition, the so-called cut-off energy threshold, the point at which the material starts to generate more electrons than it receives, improves by up to 300% in some configurations.

The researchers also subjected the coatings to six-month ageing tests and thermal treatments at 150°C, similar to those a satellite experiences when exposed to the Sun, and found that although performance drops slightly over time, it remains higher than that of freshly applied Alodine.

From patent to space, a journey that is not yet complete

The technology is already covered by a joint European patent application by CSIC and Nanostine (source in Spanish), filed with the European Patent Office in July 2025 and currently under examination.

Nanostine, a spin-off created by CSIC itself, will be responsible for commercialising the coating, aimed mainly at the aerospace sector. The development has also been funded by an Industrial PhD programme of the Community of Madrid and supported by the ESA Business Innovation Centre, coordinated in Madrid by the Madri+d Foundation.

Despite the promising results, Martínez is cautious about the timetable: taking a new coating all the way to actual use in space usually requires around a decade of testing and validation.

The researcher says ESA has expressed satisfaction with the solution put forward, but stresses that the project still has to clear several stages before these materials can fly on board a satellite.

World.title: Search called off for GB surfer who disappeared off coast of Portugal
World.content:
Authorities have called off a search for a British surfer who disappeared off the coast of Portugal earlier this week after failing to locate the missing man.

 

Arran Strong, who had competed in the World Surf League since 2016, went missing off of Arrifana beach in Portugal's southwestern Aljezur region on Monday.

According to Portugal's Autoridade Marítima Nacional (AMN), the 28-year-old had reportedly got into difficulty in the water while paddleboarding with a friend from Monte Clérigo beach to Carrapateira.

The friend, who has been identified as his coach José Maria Pyrrait, was rescued by a local fishing boat, per the AMN.

Pyrrait has shared details of the moments leading up to Strong's disappearance in a post on Instagram, writing that the pair had stopped for a drink and to take some photos as they made their way to Carrapateira.

"When we set off again, I let him go ahead," he wrote. "As I’m a faster paddler, I always did that – whenever I caught up with him and gained a short lead, I’d stop and wait for him. This time was no different, but when I stopped to wait, I saw his board drifting about 100 metres away.

Pyrrait said he then "paddled as fast as I could" to where Strong's board was and dived to look for him.

"But we were in very deep water and visibility was very poor, so I called for help from my partner on shore, who immediately alerted the rescue services," he went on. "A local fisherman picked me and the surfboards up, and we spent nearly two and a half hours scanning the entire surrounding area with the boat’s sonar."

Pyrrait added: "Arran was like a son to me; from the age of 10, he trained with me and spent his weekends and holidays with me."

"My love for him was like that for another son that life had given me."

In a post on Instagram, GB Surfing paid tribute to Strong, calling him a "fantastic teammate" and "respected competitor."

"His passing is a devastating loss to our sport and the wider surfing community, and he will be greatly missed," it said, adding: "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with Arran’s family, friends, teammates and all those whose lives he touched."

World.title: Italy: recipe for ancient elixir, possible Coca-Cola precursor, found in convent
World.content:
In the archives of the historic San Marco Pharmacy, in Florence, a mid-19th-century slip of paper has been found containing the recipe for an "Elixir vinoso ricostituente", described as a drink capable of easing physical and mental fatigue and weakness caused by age or exertion.

 

The person who found the recipe was Father Manuel Russo, rector of the San Marco convent.

"I stumbled across the old advert for this elixir while I was consulting our archive. I began delving deeper into the documentation kept in the convent and discovered that it was one of the most sought-after products in the friars' pharmacy," he told the weekly Toscana Oggi.

The composition and history of the recipe

What is most surprising is the composition of the tonic: thirty grams of kola nut and ten grams of Bolivian coca leaves, infused in a litre of alcoholic blend. It is the same mixture that underpins the medicinal compound which, in 1886, American pharmacist John Stith Pemberton is thought to have used to create his "French Wine Coca", the forerunner of modern Coca-Cola.

The only difference lies in the absence of alcohol, due to Prohibition in force in America at the time, which the pharmacist compensated for with carbonated water and syrup.

Father Manuel Russo told Toscana Oggi that the recipe dates back to the 18th century, but that it enjoyed its widest circulation between the late 19th and early 20th centuries. According to the weekly, during the period when Florence was Italy's capital, from 1865 to 1871, it was not uncommon for officials and office workers to stop at the San Marco convent during their breaks to sip the tonic.

According to the rector, this story, evidenced by the note with the recipe, some original labels and a few empty bottles, highlights the advanced pharmaceutical tradition of the Dominican friars.

As for any connection between the composition of the Florentine elixir and that of the American medicine, there is no proof whatsoever. What remains is a suggestion and a series of coincidences that arouse curiosity about the history of one of the world's most famous drinks.

The mystery of Coca-Cola's origins

Florence is not the only city where a recipe similar to that of the US beverage is hidden.

In Aielo de Malferit, a small town in Spain's Valencian Community, a very similar syrup was also produced in the 19th century, called "Nuez de Cola Coca", and it is still made today.

Originally its name was "Anís Celestial" and it was produced by the Aielo Liquor Factory, founded in 1880 by three friends, Bautista Aparici, Ricardo Sanz and Enrique Ortiz.

With their liqueurs, the owners won numerous prizes and took part in international events, including the 1889 Paris World's Fair and a drinks competition held in Philadelphia in 1885, just one year before the official birth of Coca-Cola.

"Aparici often travelled to the United States to open up new markets. In those years a blight destroyed our vineyards and he brought back a more resistant vine, the American one, which we still use today. In return he left bottles of Nuez de Cola Coca," says Juan Juan Micó, the factory's current owner, speaking to the BBC.

There is no further evidence of links between Aparici and America. What is known is that the following year pharmacist John Stith Pemberton created "French Wine Coca", which would later take the name Coca-Cola and go on to enjoy extraordinary success first in the United States and then around the world.

In the meantime, the Aielo liquor factory passed from hand to hand and, after being requisitioned during the Spanish Civil War, in 1953 it crossed paths again with the US multinational. When Coca-Cola arrived in Spain, it realised there was a similar drink hindering its expansion and it bought the patent.

Nuez de Cola Coca continues to be produced in its alcoholic version, and in Aielo de Malferit the question lingers: what if Coca-Cola really originated in a small town in the province of Valencia?

World.title: Europe wants to be a strong partner of the US in the Moon race, ESA astronaut says
World.content:
“We as Europeans, we as Italians, we want to be strong partners of the United States in this race,” astronaut Luca Parmitano told Euronews, talking about the current frontier in space exploration: returning to the Moon.

 

Parmitano, an Italian astronaut from the European Space Agency (ESA), was selected by NASA to take part in the Artemis III mission, designed to be a test mission for NASA’s Moon landing programme.

Set to launch in 2027, Artemis III will send three NASA astronauts and Parmitano to low-Earth orbit on the Orion spacecraft to dock with two lunar landers produced respectively by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin.

NASA has presented the mission as one of the most complex human spaceflights in recent history. As Parmitano prepares for it, he joined Euronews interview programme 12 Minutes With to share how he is getting on, the challenges ahead, and the current state of the space race.

Bringing the European identity into orbit

“The mission was not at all on my horizon,” said Parmitano, “I was speechless, which is quite unusual for me, and I was really grateful."

Parmitano was the first Italian commander on the International Space Station and spent over 366 days in space across two long-duration missions: Volare (2013) and Beyond (2019-2020). He was the first Italian to perform a space walk and now he will be the first European to go into orbit with the Artemis programme.

NASA publicly presented the crew for the Artemis III mission on June 9 at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. At the event, Parmitano gave an emotional speech, calling Italy his own “launch pad” and the ESA his “launch tower”.

Parmitano told Euronews he is grateful to the Italian public education system and aims to bring into orbit the spirit of determination — a characteristic of European identity for him.

“People of my age, we were not born Europeans. We became Europeans. This identity was desired, this identity has been a goal, something we wanted to achieve,” he said.

Artemis III crew member Luca Parmitano greets the crowd during a press conference at Johnson Space Center on Tuesday, June 9, 2026, in Houston. (AP Photo/Annie Mulligan) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Artemis III: a complex mission toward the Moon

Despite the excitement, Parmitano is aware of the challenges posed by Artemis III. “We have three launches that have to happen in close proximity and from very different spacecrafts,” he explained.

Multiple factors will contribute to the success of the Artemis III mission, including the readiness and successful launches of the lunar landers and NASA’s Orion spacecraft as well as the critical orbital manoeuvers.

Astronauts will also have to live in the Orion spacecraft, with a habitable volume of just 8 to 9 cubic metres. It is built for deep space conditions, which are different to those at low-Earth orbit where the mission will be conducted.

To prepare for such a complex journey, Parmitano and his three NASA crew members, Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, are now following an intense training schedule.

The programme involves practicing crucial skills, conducting simulations, and preparing for potential malfunction scenarios. “Our training is very complex and wonderfully different and varied,” Parmitano stated.

The state of the space race

If lately on Earth, relations between the EU and the US have been tense, in space, Parmitano claims, this is not the case. “We don't look at what's happening at the political level; we are operators.”

Parmitano said the Artemis III mission is part of the space race to return to the Moon and underlined that the EU-US relationship in orbit remains strong. “We all feel a common goal, which is that of the betterment of humankind on Earth, our life, and this is the next step."

The ESA has been playing an important role in the Artemis mission architecture. For example, it built the European Service Module to provide electricity, thermal control, oxygen, nitrogen, and water to the Orion spacecraft.

However, ESA's contribution to the programme was altered following NASA's decision earlier this year to pause work on the Lunar Gateway, a Moon-orbiting space station for which Europe had been building some key modules.

On the 2027 deadline, presented by many experts as far too ambitious, Parmitano argued that “to achieve complex objectives, you have to be ambitious and push hard”.

World.title: Anthropic says Claude AI hacked three companies during tests
World.content:
Three separate versions of Claude AI broke out of cybertesting environments and hacked three firms, its developer Anthropic said. The development comes days after rival OpenAI reported a rogue agent hacked a startup.

Anthropic said on Thursday that its artificial intelligence (AI) models "gained unauthorized access" to three outside organizations during testing that was supposed to be isolated from "real-world" systems.

The company reviewed 141,006 test sessions to find that three different versions of Claude, its AI model, improperly accessed the system of the three unnamed organizations.

"Claude compromised the impacted organizations' infrastructure using basic techniques, such as ‌exploiting ​weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints," Anthropic said in a blog post.

The evaluation was launched after rival OpenAI disclosed last week that itsadvanced AI models went rogue during a security test and carried out a days-long hacking spree into a digital repository of AI technology known as Hugging Face.

However, unlike the incident with OpenAI's technology, Anthropic's AI models had access to the internet due to what the company described as a "misunderstanding" with its evaluation partner Irregular, which left the systems connected to the public internet.

How did the Claude models go rogue?

The Anthropic models involved in the breach included Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research model.

Mythos 5 is one of the company's most powerful AI models which has only been released to a limited number of approved partners.

In all three incidents, Claude was tasked with a "capture the flag" challenge, which is one of the ways Anthropic assesses its models' cyber capabilities.

The company said that in the task, the model is given a fictional scenario and informed that a piece of secret information or the "flag" has been hidden on a different machine on the network. The model's objective is to break in and retrieve it.

AI under pressure: scams, security and sustainability To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anthropic said that each of the three breach incidents involved a different fictional "capture the flag" scenario.

"In one, Claude played an employee of a made-up company, attacking that company's internal systems inside a private test environment," Anthropic said in its blog.

Anthropic said it started reviewing the transcripts of its evaluation on July 23 and stopped all cyber evaluations the same day after finding evidence that Claude may have accessed the internet.

All three incidents were identified by July 24, the company said, adding that it was working with Irregular to assess the situation.

"We're approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone," Anthropic said.

Iran's military claims it had hit strategic US facilities in Kuwait, saying the drone strike was retaliation for an earlier American offensive.

Iranian forces said several drones targeted fighter jet hangars, satellite communications systems and storage facilities at Ahmed Al-Jaber Air Base in southern Kuwait.

A military statement carried by Iran's Fars news agency included footage showing drones being launched but did not say when the attack took place.

The Kuwaiti facilities had played a central role in US air and surveillance operations during the conflict, according to the Iranian military. Tehran described the base as a vital hub supporting American forces.

The Iranian military said they launched the latest strike after the US hit a home on Qeshm Island.

The island lies in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the main flashpoints between Iran and the United States.

World.title: Are Iran and Ukraine wars getting tangled in Caspian Sea?
World.content:
Tehran has threatened a response after a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was carrying weapons to Russia. Still, Ukraine says it wants to avoid escalation with Tehran.

A recent Ukrainian strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea has drawn concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine and the war in Iran are becoming entangled.

Ukraine has said the ship was carrying military equipment from Iran to Russia. Iranian state media, citing Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, reported that the cargo vessel "Anna" was anchored approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the entrance of the Volga River when it was attacked by drones causing an explosion. One sailor was reported killed.

Iran summoned Ukraine's charge d'affaires and described the incident as an act of aggression.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said Ukrainian forces had carried out successful long-range strikes against a Russian warship and vessels that Kyiv says were transporting military cargo.

Ukraine has long accused Iran of helping Russia wage war through the supply and development of Iranian-designed drones.

Tehran has acknowledged earlier drone sales to Moscow but has rejected accusations that it supplied weapons specifically for use in the Ukraine war.

However, the Ukrainian military has extensive documented physical evidence that Iranian-designed Shahed drones have been deployed throughout the war that has dragged on for more than four years.

How Ukraine shoots down Russia's drones on a budget To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In March 2026, Russia launched nearly 950 Shahed, Gerber and other types of attack drones at Ukraine in a 24-hour period, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

Iran's Foreign Ministry has accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of its war with Russia. Kyiv, by contrast, presents its attacks in the Caspian Sea as part of an effort to disrupt military logistics supporting Moscow.

Will Iran strike Ukraine?

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a statement the attack "cannot go unanswered."

However, Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, told DW that Tehran is unlikely to respond immediately with a direct military strike against Ukraine.

"I believe the Islamic Republic will avoid an emotional reaction and choose a diplomatic response instead of a military one," he said, pointing to Tehran's summoning of the Ukrainian diplomat and the possibility of raising the matter at the UN Security Council.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X that Iran's accusations were "unjustified and groundless."

"The regime in Tehran is a direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine, fueling Moscow's criminal war with weapons that have killed Ukrainians since 2022," he wrote.

A day later, in a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Sybiha softened his tone and said that Ukraine wants to avoid unnecessary escalation with Iran.

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos considers the likelihood of an Iranian retaliatory attack on Ukraine to be very low.

"Attacks on ships or ports in the Caspian Sea are one thing, since this is related to Russia," which attacked Ukraine.

"However, an Iranian missile attack on Ukrainian territory is an entirely different matter. That would be a direct act of war," said Semyvolos, adding that such an attack "would only complicate the situation for Iran."

Austrian military expert Markus Reisner told DW that an Iranian missile attack on Ukraine is unlikely, even though Tehran possesses medium-range missiles.

Reisner said it would make little sense for Iran to actually launch a missile at a target on Ukrainian territory when there could be more important or higher-value targets elsewhere.

No 'new front' in Iran war

Reisner, currently head of research at Austria's Theresian Military Academy, added that the attack in the Caspian Sea does not indicate that Ukraine is now a participant in the Iran war.

Reisner points out that the Ukrainian military has been increasing attacks on maritime facilities, particularly in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, since May. Around 200 Russian ships, tankers and tugboats have already been hit.

Ukraine's goal is not "to open a new front against Iran, but rather to disrupt supply routes between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea as well," said Reisner.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh said, however, that the attack "can be seen as a signal and an indication that the geography of the Ukrainian war is expanding from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea."

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos agrees. He finds it logical that Ukraine would expand its strategy to control sea lanes for arms deliveries and attempt to impose a general economic naval blockade against Russia in the south.

Ukrainian coordination with the US?

There is no direct evidence that the operation in the Caspian Sea was coordinated with the US, and the issue has not been publicly discussed, Semyvolos said.

"But it's obvious that Ukraine uses American intelligence data. Therefore, the Americans were most likely aware of it," Semyvolos believes.

Austrian military analyst Reisner emphasizes that the timing of Ukraine's attack plays a crucial role.

"Zelenskyy wants to clearly demonstrate here that Kyiv and Washington share a common enemy in Iran," Reisner said.

The Ukrainian attack could also be seen as a demonstration from Kyiv that it is actually a better ally in fighting Iran than some NATO countries, he added.

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, as ties between Kyiv and the Trump administration have turned positive along with Ukraine's advances on the battlefield.

Zelenskyy and Trump had perhaps their most cordial meeting so far this week in Washington Image: Zelenskyy Social Media Account/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Will Ukraine's Caspian Sea attacks continue?

As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha's statement on X indicates, Kyiv increasingly sees Iran and Russia as part of the same military ecosystem.

And Ukraine has also demonstrated tactical momentum in carrying out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian analyst Semyvolos expects Ukraine to continue its operations in the Caspian Sea. He explains the timing of the operation by noting that the Ukrainian military now has the technical ability to carry out long-range strikes.

However, if Ukraine again targets Iranian vessels, Tehran faces an uncomfortable strategic choice.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh argues that a direct Iranian military response against Ukrainian territory risks creating a new front at a time when Tehran is already confronting attacks now concentrated in southern Iran.

Vakhshiteh also suggested that Iran could instead look for indirect ways to impose costs on Ukraine, including measures against shipping connected to Ukrainian interests.

However, such options would carry their own considerable escalation risks and there is no indication that Tehran has decided to pursue them.

World.title: Spain will send troops to Ceuta to help with border security
World.content:
Authorities in the Spanish city of Ceuta asked Madrid to declare a national emergency and send military assistance. Crowds of people breached the border of the territory next to Morocco as police lost control.

Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco.

The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response."

Spain's Interior Ministry said later on Thursday that its armed forces would send personnel to Ceuta to support the border guards.

"The Armed Forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain civil security in the city of Ceuta," the ministry said.

What had happened in Ceuta during the day?

The Guardia Civil said that crowds broke through the fences into Spain after overwhelming police at the city's breakwater. Video footage showed hundreds swimming across from the Moroccan side, using inflatable inner tubes and other flotation aids.

"The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Guardia Civil in Ceuta, told the Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed."

The AFP news agency cited a spokesperson for the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta as saying that nine people had died amid the offshore rush.

The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days.

In recent days, rescue parties had already noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks.

An official from Spain's Guardia Civil policing the border described the situation as 'absolute chaos' Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What did the regional government say?

Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement.

"Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea."

The head of the regional government said its migrant reception center known as CETI had nearly a thousand people waiting outside. Here you see a much smaller crowd outside the facility on Sunday. [FILE: July 26, 2026.] Image: Antonio Sempere/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions.

"We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population."

He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult" in the territory of around 85,000 people.

How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond?

Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation.

"We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas.

"This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post.

Sanchez's Interior Ministry said that the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police were stopping "numerous people" trying to cross the border. It said that both countries had agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally."

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska made plans to visit Ceuta on Friday and evaluate the situation, the ministry said.

Why is the rush happening now?

It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue.

Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing.

The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean.

One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now.

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, at least, drew a parallel between the amnesty and Thursday's events, calling for the EU's open-border Schengen area to be "closed to Spain," and alleging that the amnesty had encouraged human trafficking.

Tajani's Spanish counterpart, Jose Luis Albares, condemned the Italian minister, saying it was "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery."

World.title: Kenya: 15 dead elephants likely poisoned by cyanide
World.content:
The elephants ate contaminated tomatoes from nearby farms. It was unclear if the poisoning was deliberate or accidental.

Wildlife officials in Kenya said on Thursday that 15 elephants found dead this month in one of the country's best-known wildlife parks were likely poisoned by cyanide.

Authorities said the poison likely originated from pesticides used on farms. The elephants lived in Amboseli National Park near the Tanzanian border.

Kenya Wildlife Service spokesperson Duncan Juma Wanyama told the AFP news agency that investigators suspect the elephants ate tomatoes contaminated with "very strong pesticides."

Officials say tomatoes were found in the stomachs of several elephants from the same herd. The animals were likely attracted to unripe plants growing on nearby farms, Wanyama added.

Unclear whether poisoning was deliberate

At least one elephant died on a farm after consuming tomatoes, while other elephants traveled towards a water source before dying days later, despite receiving treatment by vets.

Cyanide is "a toxic substance... which is very lethal, very poisonous," Wanyama said, adding that "whenever the elephant consumed it, it affects their lung and the liver."

Officials did not say who they suspected was responsible for the contamination of tomatoes at farms neighboring the Amboseli National Park.

Kenya turns to drones in elephant conservation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But it all comes as farmers have been suspected of deliberately poisoning elephants in the past, in order to prevent them from eating their crops.

Wildlife officials are investigating whether other farmers in the area use the same chemicals.

Kenya Wildlife Service has warned that such contamination could have wider consequences for livestock that also graze in the area.

"Other than the elephants and the wildlife that may be feeding in those fields, we have the local livestock. We have the goats. We have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this is truly what is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact,” Kenya Wildlife Service Director General Erustus Kanga said.

'Major setback' for conservation

Amboseli National Park is particularly known for its herds of elephants, as well as its breathtaking savannah landscapes, with Mount Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.

The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) charity said the elephant's poisoning was "a major setback" for one of Africa's key elephant populations.

IFAW said the incident highlighted the devastating impact toxic substances can have on wildlife, livestock, people and ecosystems.

"Those responsible must be held fully accountable under the law," IFAW Kenya director Ben Wandago said.

"This tragedy also underscores the urgent need for the strict control and responsible handling of highly toxic substances to prevent them from entering the natural environment," Wandago added.
