World.title: Teens flout social media ban, report says, citing lack of age checks
World.content:
More than eight in 10 Australian teenagers are still using social media three months after the government's landmark ban on the platforms for under-16s took effect because the tech firms failed to implement effective age checks, the country's internet regulator has found.

In a study published on Friday, eSafety also found most children aged between 10 and 15 were using social media just as frequently in March as they had before the ban came into force on December 10, while parental awareness of their habits decreased.

Children continued to use social media even as account ownership declined from 52 per cent to 42 per cent, with "statistically significant" reductions across YouTube, Snapchat and TikTok in particular, the report said.

Fifty-eight per cent of teenagers have reported using social media daily or more often. (Reuters: Jeremy Piper)

"Most under-16s who had social media accounts before commencement were able to either retain them or create new ones at the three-month mark, with social media platforms' failure to implement effective age assurance measures cited as the main reason," eSafety said in a statement.

Australia introduced the world-first ban because of concerns about the impact of social media on the mental and physical health of children and young people.

Its implementation is being closely watched by many nations that have since sought to introduce their own curbs.

Before the ban, nearly 86 per cent of children surveyed reported using at least one age-restricted platform.

Three months later, that figure remained above 81 per cent, the report said.

About 58 per cent of teenagers reported using social media daily or more often, barely down from about 60 per cent before the ban, it found.

The report showed minimal change in "sports and physical activity, arts and music, spending time with friends and family, and attendance at community events".

Teens say their ages not checked

Around half of the children who retained their accounts said platforms had not checked their age; the most common reason they were able to stay on the services.

Others said their accounts listed them as aged 16 or older or that age-checking systems had incorrectly determined they were older.

The findings broadly matched snapshot data eSafety published in late March.

eSafety says it will investigate possible non-compliance by ​five platforms. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

After the March update, eSafety announced it was investigating possible non-compliance by ​five platforms: Meta's Facebook and Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and Google's YouTube.

The government said in June it would double the ​maximum penalty on tech firms that failed to uphold the ban, and strengthen eSafety's information-gathering powers.

"While eSafety has observed some improvements by industry since its March social media minimum age update, concerns remain about the compliance of the five platforms named at that time," the regulator said.

Meta, Snapchat, TikTok and Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The report, prepared by a global advisory panel of university researchers, compared data collected from more than 4,000 children and families before the ban started and three months later.

It is the first report to be released as part of a two-year study to evaluate the outcomes of the world-first ban.

While some children surveyed before the ban took effect said they expected negative mental health effects, more than 65 per cent said the ban had had no impact, the data showed.

Social media ban spreads More and more countries are following Australia's lead and introducing social media bans for children, but US policies are piecemeal and vary from state to state.

The report also noted an increase in children's use of messaging platforms and online gaming.

The number of children using Reddit rose from 6 per cent to more than 9 per cent, with or without an account, noted the report.

Reddit, which is included in the ban and challenging its inclusion in the High Court, was not immediately available for comment.

The ban could also be creating unintended consequences, including a decline in parental awareness of children's use of social media, the report said.

"This dynamic may have implications for help-seeking behaviours and the identification of online harms, as reduced parental awareness could limit opportunities for support or early intervention," it said.

Reuters

World.title: Elderly woman dies after two-hour wait for Victorian ambulance
World.content:
An elderly woman in Melbourne's west died after waiting two hours for paramedics to arrive after a Triple Zero call was triggered.

Ambulance Victoria (AV) chief executive Jordan Emery said the woman had a fall in her Hoppers Crossing home on Friday morning but was not attended to for hours.

"Ambulance Victoria was in a period of significant operational demand and attended that incident approximately two hours after the first initial call was received," Mr Emery said.

He promised a "comprehensive review" around the incident and said AV was still not aware of the full circumstances around the woman's death.

Jordan Emery says an investigation is still to be conducted into the circumstances around the death. (ABC News: James Oaten)

Mr Emery said the ambulance service was being subjected to a period of "heightened demand" in recent weeks.

"That demand has been consistent with other evenings and mornings over the last couple of weeks," Mr Emery said.

"We have seen an increase in acuity at various hospitals across Melbourne and the state.

"We have seen an increase in sickness in our own workforce as a result of winter illness."

Mr Emery said 12 additional crews had been rostered on in recent days to cope with the demand.

He said AV had been in contact with the woman's family and offered his sincere condolences.

Victoria Police are now preparing a report for the coroner following the death of the Hoppers Crossing woman.

"A woman aged in her 90s was located deceased inside the property on Rudolph Street about 7am," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

"The death is not being treated as suspicious."

A Triple Zero Victoria spokesperson said the initial emergency call from an alarm company was answered immediately and passed onto Ambulance Victoria.

"There were no delays in TZV answering or actioning the alarm company's 000 [Triple Zero] call, which was answered within seconds and referred to AV's secondary triage services team based on the information provided by the caller and in accordance with AV’s protocols," the spokesperson said.

Triple Zero Victoria says there was no delay in passing on the emergency call to Ambulance Victoria. (ABC News)

Victoria's Triple Zero system was overhauled in 2022 and rebranded following widespread failures.

A review conducted from October 2021 to May 2022 of the state's Emergency Services Telecommunications Authority found at least 12 people died in the period while while waiting for an ambulance.

The review saw the service rebranded as Triple Zero Victoria and $333 million invested by the government into improving the system and hiring more call-takers.

World.title: Court overturns decision to exclude video in trial of ex-Sydney nurses
World.content:
Video evidence previously ruled inadmissible will be allowed in the trial of two former Sydney nurses accused of making menacing comments about Israelis, following a Court of Appeal judgement.

Two former Bankstown Hospital nurses, Sarah Abu Lebdeh and Ahmad Rashad Nadir, have pleaded not guilty to using a carriage service to menace and harass, following a conversation with an Israeli influencer on the cam chat app Chatruletka in February last year.

Ms Abu Lebdeh has pleaded not guilty to an additional charge of threatening violence to a group, after allegedly making threats to Israeli patients during the chat.

Ms Abu Lebdeh (wearing all brown) has pleaded not guilty to an additional charge of threatening violence to a group. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Defence lawyers for the pair had argued the video chat itself should be excluded from the case because it was improperly obtained and breached privacy laws.

Last month, the District Court of NSW ruled in their favour.

But prosecutors took the matter to the Court of Appeal, which on Friday overturned that decision, meaning the unedited video is no longer inadmissible evidence.

Reasons for the judgement have been handed to the parties to consider what parts should be subject to suppression or non-publication orders ahead of the trial.

They cannot be published until further order of the court.

Video's country of origin disputed

During a day's worth of legal argument in the Court of Appeal last week, barristers for the Crown and the former nurses argued about which country the video was technically recorded in.

Barrister for the Crown, Paul Holdenson KC, argued the recording was created by influencer Max Veifer, whose real name is Max Ilinsky, in Israel, and therefore it did not break any NSW laws.

"Mr Ilinsky was sitting in Israel at the time of the conversation," he told the court.

"His computer was with him in Israel."

Lawyers for the former nurses wanted the judge's decision to exclude the evidence to remain in place.

Mr Nadir pleaded not guilty to using a carriage service to menace and harass. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Defence barrister Peter Lange SC argued the offence was partly committed in NSW because the former nurses' computer had a microphone to record the conversation.

"What was used was the microphone in the room at the hospital … in order to capture the sound," he said.

"The conversation may also have been in Israel … but it is also in New South Wales."

Mr Holdenson told the hearing the Crown case would be significantly impacted if it could not use the video, because the jury would not have a proper understanding of the context of the conversation.

"The jury can only do that if the jury can see and hear what was said … and the tone and manner in which is it was said, together with any hand gestures and expressions," he said.

"Without the video … the crown case is indeed very, very much weakened."

The former nurses, who were sacked after the incident, are due to stand trial at the end of August.

World.title: Why farmers are spreading crushed glass on their crops
World.content:
A growing number of Australian farmers are spraying or spreading pulverised glass on their paddocks to boost the productivity of their soils, plants and livestock.

Victorian agronomist Peter Norwood has been recommending the Queensland made organic product to clients for several years.

"There could be as much as 25 or 30 per cent improvements in plant growth and plant productivity," Mr Norwood said.

"We've got the potential for greater milk production, and in beef and sheep, we've got potential for greater daily body weight gain.

"This is a bit of a game changer," he said.

Ceramic balls are used to grind recycled glass into fine agricultural-grade particles. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

It is a win for the environment as the source material is glass bottles from Queensland recycler Containers for Change which pays people 10 cents for their glass empties.

Turning waste glass into farming gold

The pulverised glass is turned into an agricultural product at a new $4 million factory in Brisbane co-owned by agronomist David Archer and a group of investors.

A 60 tonne ceramic lined cylindrical tumbler filled with 35 tonnes of fist sized ceramic balls breaks the glass down into a variety of sizes which are applied to crops and pastures.

Agronomist David Archer said he discovered the benefits of silicon by accident during plant trials. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

Some farmers mix the talc-like powder with water and spray it on their plants, while others prefer spreading dry granules.

Mr Archer discovered the benefits accidentally, after doing some plant trials.

"Like most great ideas it was by accident, we were fiddling around with some glass material many moons ago, threw some in, and it was like Jack and the Beanstalk," he said.

Mr Archer explained improvements in plant yields, soil health and animal weight gains are due to silicon, a chemical component of glass.

Discarded glass bottles are the raw material used to produce the final silicon product. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Silicon protects a plant against pests and disease and drought by stimulating its natural defences, its immune system if you like," he said.

It is a bonus for the bottom line too, as the farmers using it do not need to apply as much fertiliser.

That is because silicon unlocks elements in the soil that are 'locked up', and unavailable to plants.

"In the soil a good quality silicon will attract iron, so what happens is the iron will move away from the phosphate, releasing it so the roots can get at it," Mr Archer explained.

How silicon helps unlock nutrients in the soil

Mr Norwood said seeing farmers getting access to fertiliser they have paid for which is sitting unused in their soils is exciting.

"Silicon is king, it releases the phosphates back to the plants and encourages all the nitrogen fixing bacteria in the soil," Mr Norwood said.

Agronomist Peter Norwood (left) with client Tony Donovan, who has trialled silicon on the dairy and beef operations he manages. (ABC Landline: Kyle Harley)

" We've got an opportunity to create some free nitrogen for the plants too, so there's a few wins all in one package there. "

The Brisbane factory trucks out 20 tonnes of ground glass, powder and granules a week to farmers growing apples, wine grapes, grain, cane, dairy and beef around the country.

One of Peter Norwood's clients, Warrnambool farm manager Tony Donovan sprayed silicon on a third of the 14,000 hectares he manages for Midfield Meats' dairy and beef operations.

Partially processed recycled glass on its way to be broken down to a talc-like powder or fine granules. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

"Ten years ago if you'd talked to me about silicon I would have said, 'what's that?'" he laughed.

"It's quite amazing to think the research has been done on it now for some 70, 80, 90 years and the benefits have been shown, yet it hasn't been incorporated into our standard agronomy."

Weight gains surprise beef producers

He said the performance of his beef cattle over winter surprised everyone.

"We've taken winter weight gains from 0.7, 0.8 a day to 1.4, and up to 2 kilos a day, they're big percentages and grass growth, I've got to say we're measuring in the same way."

Dairy cows on a Midfield Meats property where silicon has been trialled to improve pasture productivity and livestock performance. (Supplied)

When the Iran war slowed international shipping earlier this year imported fertiliser supplies in Australia slowed and prices soared.

That vulnerability has made the search for home-grown alternatives a financial imperative.

Mr Donovan said adding silicon is one of several management changes he has made to reduce reliance on imported urea (nitrogen fertiliser).

He said silicon will play a bigger role in coming years.

The Brisbane facility processes glass collected through Queensland's Containers for Change scheme. (Getty Images)

"We're getting bold enough now to step out and say, 'hey we're going to have a real proper go with all of this because we're getting the difference that we are looking for.'"

Mr Donovan said he does not need to feel too guilty about drinking wine.

" That empty bottle of wine you can look at it and say 'you good thing go on and contribute to the health of the land and the future of the planet.' "

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm AEST on Sunday or stream anytime on ABC iview.

World.title: Education union threatens August 19 strike without teacher pay deal
World.content:
The Australian Education Union says its members will stop work for 24 hours next month if the Victorian government does not return to the negotiating table with a better offer.

Australian Education Union (AEU) Victorian branch president Justin Mullaly said despite media reports, the Carroll government had not engaged with the union about improving the previous offer.

"We demand that the government come back and negotiate. We need to see them put a revised offer," he said.

"We need to see them sign a full funding deal with the Commonwealth.

"If that doesn't happen, then members will stop work, right around the state, for 24 hours on Wednesday the 19th of August."

The announced strike on August 19 will be the third this year for Victorian public school teachers. (ABC News: Toby Hussey)

Mr Mullaly said the union was negotiating with the government up until it made its last offer on July 17.

He said since the changes in government this week, which elevated former education minister Ben Carroll to the office of Victorian premier, it was unclear who would lead negotiations as the new education minister.

Mr Mullaly said the union was prepared to sit down to negotiate with whoever the new minister was.

"The union has made it clear both publicly and otherwise we will engage in discussions whenever and wherever the government wishes to do that," he said.

" We stand ready. Is [Ben Carroll] ready? He needs to be. "

Mr Mullaly said union members had indicated they were prepared to take further industrial action to force the government back to the bargaining table.

The ABC has contacted the Department of Education for comment.

Protracted negotiations between the state government and Victorian teachers have stretched on for more than a year.

In June, Victorian teachers went against AEU advice and voted down a pay rise of between 28 and 32 per cent.

In March, teachers and supporters took strike action statewide, marching to parliament in central Melbourne, with police estimating 35,000 people were in attendance.

Last Friday, a second strike was held, with an estimated 20,000 people in attendance.

Mr Mullaly said a range of other industrial actions were continuing, including reduced meetings and a moratorium on responding to departmental emails.

World.title: NT school back in community hands after year of statutory management
World.content:
An independent Indigenous school in Alice Springs is back under community management after 12 months of statutory arrangements.

Yipirinya School was put in the hands of administrators in July last year amid significant financial issues and after former principal Gavin Morris was charged with assaulting students.

Greg Hollis says it is important to deliver a quality education to as many students as possible. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Principal Greg Hollis said the school was focused on "teaching and learning" to rebuild student numbers, which would increase funding and help the school repay $3.7 million to the federal government.

"If we're bringing in significant numbers but we're not actually providing the quality education they deserve, then we're doing them a disservice," he said.

"I want to encourage them to come along, to attend regularly and to learn. That's where it is at the moment."

Mr Hollis said about 186 students were enrolled at the school, which had a 51 per cent attendance rate most days.

Stuart Reid says the school will pay off the debt over the next five years. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Former administrator Stuart Reid said Yipirinya School would make its first debt repayment at the start of next year.

"The way it works is that the government will retain the sum of around about $700,000 from each year's funding, so it's not cash going back, it's just less cash coming to the school," he said.

"We've budgeted for that, so the school will be able to manage that over that five-year period."

Yipirinya School needs to pay back $3.7 million to the federal government. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

Mr Hollis said the schools funding would be spent as wisely as possible.

"We'll be able to direct it appropriately to ensure that we maximise the learning outcomes … if we stay with that, I'm pretty sure we can manage and do a good job at the same time," he said.

Committee aims to regain trust

The new Yipirinya School Committee has been formed by nine people: Beverley Angeles, Cherisse Buzzacott, Kumalie Kngwarraye, Shirleen Campbell, Kate Mar Fan, Mathew Axeton, Neil McLeod, Dominic McCormack and Jake Quinlivan.

Ms Kngwarraye said the school was founded on the basis of Indigenous people passing on knowledge and two-way learning.

"This is a very important time celebrating the hand-back to the community for self-management and control, self-determination and empowerment for our people to look after our own affairs," she said.

Kate Mar Fan and Kumalie Kngwarraye say the committee has its work cut out for it, but are optimistic about the future. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Ms Mar Fan said the committee needed to rebuild community trust.

"It's definitely not going to be easy, but we're definitely going to be trying our hardest to work through everything that we can for the best outcome for our students and our staff," she said.

World.title: Silos lit up in pink as rural Victorian town farewells allegedly murdered 13-year-old girl
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Silos lit up in pink as rural Victorian town farewells allegedly murdered 13-year-old girl Lachlan Abbott July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Silos glowed pink and bubbles floated across a simple white coffin as the small country town of Donald gathered to remember a young life cut short. Hundreds of mourners from across the farming region in the state’s north-west attended Friday’s public memorial for 13-year-old Layla Jeffery, who was allegedly murdered by another child earlier this month. Donald teenager Layla Jeffery, whose body was one of four Australian women and girls allegedly murdered in four days in July. Police Media Bunches of pink balloons escorted Layla’s coffin outside before it was driven through a guard of honour in heart of the historic town of 1400 people. “Layla was a truly spectacular person who would have conquered the world if she hadn’t been taken from us,” said Layla’s aunt, Kaitlyn Cheyne, who delivered the eulogy.



Attendees at Layla’s memorial service were asked to wear a black hoodie or a Hello Kitty item to honour her. Layla’s father, Aaron, also read out a tribute. Her friends wrote messages on her coffin. An emotional compilation of photos was played. And, overnight, Donald’s grain silos were lit up in pink in Layla’s memory. The small community was rocked on Friday, July 10 when police searching for Layla announced they had discovered a body near the Richardson River the day before. Authorities had launched a major search after Layla was last seen on Saturday, July 4, and reported missing by a family member the next day. A 16-year-old boy from northern Victoria, who cannot be identified as he is a child, was charged with Layla’s murder on July 11.



Born in Shepparton in 2013, Layla spent time in Benalla and moved to Donald three years ago, her aunt said. “Though her years were far shorter than she deserved, over that time she grew into someone who felt a deep love for her family and friends, with a strong sense of self and the confidence to back it up,” Cheyne said. The silos in Donald were lit up in pink in honour of Layla Jeffery. Facebook “Though she was also something of a paradox because she often disliked being perceived, and liked to simply exist quietly alongside those she loved most.” Cheyne recalled the sounds of laughter when Layla had sleepovers with her friends, and fondly remembered her love of fashion, particularly jewellery and colouring her hair.



Layla always looked out for her friends and had a brilliant creative streak, Cheyne said. She loved her pets, music, movies like the Harry Potter series, and TV shows like Brooklyn Nine-Nine. “She was both shy and confident in many different ways – funny, sassy, kind, generous, stylish, sweet, cheeky, loving, and considerate,” her aunt said. Layla’s aunt, Kaitlyn Cheyne, speaks outside the family home earlier this month. Ashleigh McMillan “And I could go on and on and on, but it would still never be enough words to express the depth of her character or the loss we are all feeling.” The boy charged with Layla’s murder was due to face a children’s court on Friday, but his case was adjourned beforehand until late August.

World.title: ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced
World.content:
CultureArt & designVisual art ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced Elizabeth Flux July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Robert Fielding enters the room, he quietly takes in all the different artworks. His own is hung in one corner, but he walks straight up to another nearby – Minymaku Inma by Betty Campbell – then sits on the floor beneath it. He then makes his way across to Ngangkari Ngura (Healing Country) by Betty Muffler and does the same. Both artists, like Fielding, work in the APY Lands – and Campbell, like Fielding, works with Mimili Maku Arts. Hadley’s Art Prize 2026 winner Robert Fielding with his work Landscape. Jessica King Fielding’s work Landscape has been announced as the 2026 winner of the $100,000 Hadley’s Art Prize. He was first told the news over the phone, and now sitting in the gallery, his eyes start to fill with tears as recalls the moment he heard he had won. “I cried with tears of joy,” he says. “I had no words – and the two people came into my mind: my mum and my dad. Because when you see my artwork, it’s all about stolen generations.” It’s been a big year for the artist in an already soaring career. His portrait Tjintir-Tjintir was a finalist in this year’s Archibald, and Heritage impact assessment was a finalist in the Wynne prize.



Landscape is a scene that is mostly rendered in burnt red. Rundown cars are stacked on top of each other, tyres missing, doors open, windows gone. Down one side runs the word “Sacred”. Across the top reads “Nganampa” – ours. For Fielding, whose work also spans printmaking and photography, abandoned cars are a recurring motif, as vessels that house memory. “This is telling you a story of land … I’m very harsh with myself because when I paint, I paint for people,” he says. “I paint for movement. I paint for what was inside those relics. Who owned them? Who did they belong to?” he says. “They became heritage.” Run through Hobart’s Hadley’s Orient Hotel, the prize is one of the country’s richest for visual arts. This year, it was judged by Abdul Abdullah, Judith Ryan and Sarah Wallace. Works by Imants Tillers, Betty Muffler and Mia Boe. Jessica King



“It’s a very traditional mark-making process to tell a very contemporary and forward-looking story,” says Abdullah. “What drew me to it, even before we got into the room, was the way he wrote about it and his explanation.” Fielding’s work, Abdullah adds, “was interrogating landscape in a way that was unique in the prize”. Wallace says: “It’s a familiar sight that you see in a lot of places across Australia. But for him, it wasn’t something ugly or a blight on the landscape; it held memory and stories of Country, and travelling across Country.” The 26 finalist works on display at Hadley’s, in a pop-up downstairs gallery, offer a fascinating insight not only into the Australian landscape, but how it is perceived through different eyes. Walking through the exhibition, curator Dr Amy Jackett highlights details of each work. Bunuru Nocturne, Derbal yerrigan (High-Summer Night, Swan River) by Kelsey Ashe Jessica King



One of the few works on paper is watercolour and collage work Entanglement by Grace Gladdish. Emerald Coral by Ken Done is so vibrant it spills off the canvas and onto the frame. The winner of the prize’s residency award, Bunuru Nocturne, Derbal Yerrigan (High-Summer Night, Swan River) by Kelsey Ashe, is already unusual in that it depicts the landscape at night, then Jackett picks up a UV torch that makes the bioluminescent pigments glow wherever the light hits. Trill by Natasha Bieniek is so small and detailed it will be presented with a magnifying glass. The climate emergency is a recurring theme across the exhibition. Joe Blundell’s Tormented Land shows a scene of fallen trees, with the dirt between them littered with tracks of heavy machinery. It’s an idea that also drove Alice Mannheim’s work Log It!, which was awarded the Packing Room Prize. “I wanted to show that these environments are disappearing because people are destroying them through logging and deforestation,” Mannheim says. “I chose the Daintree rainforest because it’s very beautiful, but it’s also at risk of being destroyed.” Artist Alice Mannheim pictured with her work Log It! At 19, she is the prize’s youngest finalist, and this is the first time she has put her work forward for an award. She cites Harold Thornton’s portrait of Bob Brown, Dr Brown and Green Old Time Waltz, 1983, as an influence. She says that living in Canberra, “I’ve always been drawn to it.”



Her work is predominantly painted from memory, and she says: “I chose the title Log It! because it’s such a simple statement describing a simple action, but it has a very devastating impact.” The irony is deliberate – the beauty and detail of the rainforest versus the ease in which it can be eradicated. All the works – with the exception of Fielding’s, which has been acquired by Hadley’s – are for sale. “The prize to me means many things,” says Fielding. “It means many opportunities. I’m already planning.” For Fielding, this win is meaningful beyond a personal victory, and he emphasises the importance of paving the way for the next generation of artists and his work with Mimili Maku Arts in the APY Lands. “We’re here as a team, Mimili Maku Arts [to show] that art centres are our hub, our heartbeat, our unison, our grief, our sorrow, our finance, our fighting dream,” he says. “But most of all, it’s about respect.” The Hadley’s Art Prize exhibition is on at Hadley’s Orient Hotel, Hobart, from August 1-23.

World.title: Bush trainer’s $5000 birthday gift ready to upstage $3m rival
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Bush trainer’s $5000 birthday gift ready to upstage $3m rival Craig Kerry July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tony Ball saw plenty of expensive horse flesh during his decade-long stint as a foreman for Godolphin in Sydney, and he knows first hand that breeding and price tags can often mean little when it comes to how they perform on the racetrack. That’s partly why the Taree trainer has no qualms about taking $5000 buy Andrea to Rosehill for a first crack at Saturday city company, after he was balloted out of the Highway Handicap for country-trained horses. Andrea, right, tries to catch Sneaky Pee Cee in the Highway Handicap at Rosehill on July 18. Shannen Llewellyn rides him again on Saturday. Getty Images Coming off an eye-catching second in a Highway last start, Andrea will take on a field including Chris Waller-trained $3 million filly Ernaux, a daughter of I Am Invincible and Booker which has shown promise in city company but won only one race in 14 starts in the colours of American billionaire John Stewart. Ball has worked at both ends of the breeding and training spectrum. He enjoyed his time as a foreman under the leadership of Peter Snowden, John O’Shea and briefly James Cummings with Darley and Godolphin before later training his own team in the country.



“You see them come and you see them go, and everyone says they’ve got slow ones,” Ball said of the racing powerhouse. “Well, let me tell you, everyone’s got slow ones.” Trainer Tony Ball. Getty Images Ball now trains a team of 25 and he had 15 winners in the 2025-26 season, including a Canterbury victory with The Face. Xtra Approval gave him his other city winner in 2022 in a Rosehill Highway. He hopes Andrea can go a step higher to kick off the new season. The Graff gelding was held up briefly for a run last start before motoring home to almost catch Sneaky Pee Cee in a class 2 1100m Highway two weeks ago on heavy going. A $6 TAB chance, he steps up to 1200m on Saturday for a benchmark 72 handicap for three and four-year-olds.



“If you look at it, they are only class 3 horses, so it’s the same as the Highway,” Ball said. “And there’s only 10 in it now. He’ll go good and you never know. You can try him and just see how he goes. “If you’re not in it, you can’t win it, and he’s run third in a 64 in Sydney before. He’s consistent and he tries. He runs them down, he really finishes off. “There’s another Highway in a couple of weeks we might be able to get into. If he wins, we’ll just go day by day, that’s our attitude.” The bargain buy from the 2024 Inglis Classic Yearling Sale, owned by Ball’s wife, Barbara, and son, Michael, has two wins and four placings in 12 starts for a return of $75,338.



“I wish they were all like that,” Ball said. “My wife actually bought him for my son for his 40th birthday, and you are never going to believe why they bought him. “My wife loves Kitchwin Hill horses, and he had the KWH on him, and she saw him. “We’ve had quite a few of them and we’ve had luck with them, so we just keep picking one out occasionally and buy them. “We’ve got a stable full of young ones and you never know what’s around the corner for them.”



Related Article Horse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Rosehill on Saturday Scone stud Kitchwin Hills famously foaled and raised Melbourne Cup winner Vow And Declare and Everest champion Yes Yes Yes. Ball has fond memories of his time with Darley and Godolphin, which started out of the blue. “I was training in Queensland and my wife saw a job advertised and put in for it. I didn’t even know about it,” he said. “We got it, so we went down to Warwick Farm. We had a great time there and met some really nice people, and we’re still friends with them all down there. Brad Widdup was an assistant trainer and I worked under him, and I’m still great mates with him.”

World.title: ‘Trade friction’: Beijing is turning up the heat on Australian iron ore
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMining ‘Trade friction’: Beijing is turning up the heat on Australian iron ore Nick Toscano Updated July 31, 2026 — 4:56pm ,first published 2:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billionaire Andrew Forrest’s Fortescue Metals Group has become the latest major mining company targeted by China’s push to force down iron ore prices, putting future revenue from Australia’s most valuable export commodity under pressure. Fortescue, the nation’s third-largest iron ore producer, on Friday confirmed it was locked in contract discussions with China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG), Beijing’s centralised buyer created to leverage the country’s massive purchasing power against foreign suppliers. Fortescue’s Cloudbreak mine in Western Australia. Fortescue insisted it would continue to push for a swift return to normal market-led conditions despite mounting pressure from Beijing. “It’s the latest example of trade friction affecting the iron ore industry, undermining the stable supply of iron ore to China,” Gus Pichot, Fortescue’s chief executive of growth and energy, told analysts on Friday.



“We hope to see a return to normal market conditions as soon as possible.” Iron ore, the key raw material use to make steel, is Australia’s single biggest export, generating more than $100 billion a year in export earnings, meaning even a minor decline in pricing could have a significant impact on state and federal government revenue and the broader economy. Andrew Forrest speaking at Boao Forum in Perth on Monday. Ross Swanborough Iron ore routinely accounts for as much as 5 per cent of Australia’s gross domestic product. China is the biggest buyer of the commodity from Australia by far. However, the stand-off over pricing and future supply terms with Fortescue presents the latest test of China’s attempt to use its enormous purchasing power to drive down the cost of iron ore. Since its establishment in 2022, CMRG has sought to consolidate the bargaining power of Chinese steel mills in contract negotiations with suppliers, including Australia’s BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue.



Fortescue has declined to confirm or deny reports, published in Reuters and Bloomberg, that suggest Beijing has told steel mills and traders to restrict or delay imports of some of Fortescue’s specific iron ore products in a bid to gain leverage. Related Article Mining Australia’s miners were racing to decarbonise. Why are some tapping the brakes? BHP, the largest Australian mining company, came under pressure from CMRG during contract negotiations last year. According to media reports at the time, CMRG ordered Chinese steel to halt any new dollar-denominated purchase deals for BHP iron ore. Speaking at an event in Perth last week, Forrest did not mention CMRG, but said Australia had never been a “fair-weather friend” to China, and implored the two countries to “always negotiate fairly”. “Together we built mines, we built railways, we built the ports of the Pilbara. Together, we built the iron ore industry that supports nearly 400,000 jobs and many, many more families directly and indirectly,” he said.



“Each nation becomes stronger as each succeeds.” Fortescue on Friday said it continued to engage in respectful, patient and good-faith negotiations with CMRG, but a return to “normal market conditions” would be the best outcome for Chinese steel mills and their Australian trade partners that had been their reliable suppliers for decades. The company said China remained its major market, but it would also continue exploring alternative destinations for its iron ore, such as major growth economies of South-East Asia and India. China, Australia’s biggest trading partner, has appeared increasingly willing to use its market clout to exert pressure on its suppliers of key commodities. In 2020, Beijing slapped an unofficial ban on Australian coal amid a diplomatic stoush with then-prime minister Scott Morrison, leaving dozens of coal ships stranded at sea for months, unable to dock at Chinese ports. Meanwhile, the Yindjibarndi, the traditional landowners in WA’s Pilbara, said this week they were preparing to launch an appeal against a recent Federal Court ruling that Fortescue must pay them $150 million in compensation for mining their ancestral land without an agreement and damaging dozens of cultural sites. Following a community meeting in Roebourne, the Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation, which had initially been seeking $1.8 billion from Fortescue, on Thursday said it would lodge an appeal over the amount awarded.



“Ultimately, the members decided today that having come this far, the only option was to keep fighting,” Yindjibarndi Group chief executive Michael Woodley said. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ASX Runners of the Week: H2G Limited, Carnaby & American Tungsten
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: H2G Limited, Carnaby & American Tungsten Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd July 31, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What a wild ride in markets this week. Following Trump’s latest TACO (Trump always chickens out) over the weekend, the market basically spent four days further unwinding the lofty market capped AI majors, on building fears of inflation and deepening concerns of an escalating war in the Middle East. But then it was a case of whiplash Friday, led as always by US markets after Microsoft jump a half-trillion-dollars in valuation, the largest single day gain by any company in history. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… H2G Limited. The ultimate bait and switch came as tech stocks spent much of the month getting belted, with mega market cappers like Nvidia caught up in the semiconductor sell-off, down more than 6 per cent just this week. Big tech and its big expectations are now caught between potential future revenues vs the capex/energy costs of its data centre developments.



But, those worries were squashed on Friday as Microsoft arrived with a 43 per cent surge in its Azure cloud unit revenue and promptly bowing a hole through every bear argument going. Shares in Microsoft rocketed more than 16 per cent, adding almost US$450 billion (A$640 billion) to its market value in a single session, the biggest one-day gain by any company in market history. The rally dragged the Nasdaq up 2.8 per cent and sent semiconductor stocks flying, with battlers like Micron gaining 18 per cent, putting the AI bleed on hold - at least for a day or two. Thanks to missiles still flying over the Strait of Hormuz, oil remained as volatile as it has been since the fracas with Iran kicked off. Those market conditions look to have been the principle reason the US Federal Reserve left rates on hold with inflation concerns very much front and centre. That’s not exactly the backdrop you want when the world’s most expensive and energy hungry technology stocks are being priced on growth rates a decade into the future. Amazingly back in Australia, the ASX finally got some inflation relief. Annual CPI eased to 3.8 per cent in June – but try explaining that to Aussie households. So yes, inflation is moving in the right direction, but not nearly fast enough for anyone to start flirting with the words rate cut, especially not with a buzzword “energy security” lurking in the shadows of the US-Iran war. The Australian Government amazingly opened its eyes to its recent oil woes this week, proposing a WA oil refinery to be added to the energy security mix. The petrol refinery would be Australia’s third, adding to existing facilities in Brisbane and Geelong, and the first domestic refinery to be constructed since the 1960s.



Meanwhile, the strange safe haven in copper is becoming an increasingly important profit engine for our mining majors. Rio Tinto delivered a 43 per cent jump in first-half underlying earnings, sending it and BHP up more than 2 per cent a piece on Friday, to start out a promising reporting season. Higher copper prices don’t just make existing mines more profitable - they are completely changing the economics of projects that were previously parked in the far too-hard basket, creating a rather tasty takeover landscape. The big miners don’t necessarily need another billion-dollar greenfield megaproject. They can buy established brownfield assets in Tier-1 jurisdictions and plug them into existing infrastructure to potentially bring production online far faster and cheaper. Of course, not every major miner had a perfect week. Fortescue had to flag an approximately US$750 million (A$1.07 billion) pre-tax impairment on its troubled Iron Bridge magnetite operation. Our Runners were once again few and far between this week. So dire is the small caps volumes that our top spot was taken out by a bounce back candidate after a rough couple of months, as hundreds of millions was splurged on some Aussie copper juniors, who are beginning to pop their heads up.



H2G LIMITED (ASX: H2G) Up 133% (0.6c – 1.4c) Taking out Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is renewable energy storage solutions group H2G Limited. There was no news on the week for the renewable tech maestro, however, the company was handed a speeding ticket from market overlords down at the ASX on Wednesday after its share price curiously doubled, increasing from 0.7 cents to 1.4c on no announcements. In response, H2G said it was unaware of any foul play, instead noting a rather hefty material shareholder had been selling down its position over the past few months.



A big shareholder holding down the sell button for some time can quash any hopes of making a penny and it seems the one-way share price traffic may have finally let up. With the big seller now out of the way, the company cheekily noted the current share price is still below levels it was trading at just a couple of months ago. H2G bills itself as one of Australia’s leading innovators in the delivery of engineering solutions for renewable energy. In its last quarterly report, H2G mentioned the launch of the H2G PowerSafe Sodium-Ion Battery Range. The H2G PowerSafe Sodium-Ion Battery range is designed for residential, commercial, industrial and utility applications. Engineered specifically for Australian conditions, the company says its batteries provide a safe, affordable, long-life and sustainable energy storage.



H2G says it is in discussion with large-scale industrial users for its sodium-ion batteries, particularly where safety is the prime goal, giving investors a glimpse of the commercialisation pathway ahead now that the seller-induced handbrake appears to be off. Carnaby Resources’ Greater Duchess copper-gold project, near Cloncurry in northwest Queensland. CARNABY RESOURCES LTD (ASX: CNB) Up 66% (48c – 79.5c) Snagging silver this week is junior copper developer Carnaby Resources, after Evolution Mining swooped in to scoop up the company in a takeover deal that could put its Greater Duchess copper project into production.



Under the proposed scheme, Carnaby shareholders were offered 0.0682 Evolution shares for every Carnaby share, valuing the deal at around 77 cents a share based on Evolution’s $11.29 closing price. The 77c represents a serious premium for Carnaby and its board has unanimously backed the transaction, in the absence of a superior proposal. The attraction is obvious. Carnaby’s Greater Duchess copper-gold project hosts a 29 million tonne resource grading 1.5 per cent copper equivalent for 441,000 tonnes of contained copper equivalent, sitting in the heart of Queensland’s historic Cloncurry copper district. Carnaby had been progressing a feasibility study based around toll-treating its ore through Glencore’s processing infrastructure. Evolution has a much simpler trick up its sleeve: process the ore through its nearby Ernest Henry operation, dumping the need for the Glencore tolling and offtake arrangements and potentially turning a stranded development into a low-capex copper opportunity. Evolution’s move is a textbook example of the brownfield takeover wave gathering pace across the resources sector. Yesterday’s uneconomic deposit in a Tier-1 mining district, becomes tomorrow’s money churner.



When copper prices rise to the current all-time high prices, the strategic acquisitions come thick and fast, with players like Evolution betting the copper sentiment with AI is a long-term play and here to stay. American Tungsten & Antimony’s newly acquired White Spar mine in Nevada, USA. AMERICAN TUNGSTEN & ANTIMONY LTD (ASX: AT4) Up 64% (3.3c – 5.4c) Rounding out our Runners is US critical minerals dynamo American Tungsten & Antimony, which is rapidly moving beyond the explorer bucket after striking a deal to acquire the Del Sol hydrometallurgical antimony refinery in Nevada and the producing White Spar mine feeding it.



The company says its refinery is currently permitted to process up to 18,500 tonnes of feed a year, but American Tungsten isn’t mucking around targeting approvals to ramp that capacity towards 100,000 tonnes annually while also adding tungsten refining to the fold. The deal slots neatly into the company’s growing US critical minerals arsenal, alongside its flagship Antimony Canyon project in Utah and Dutch Mountain, which boasts historic tungsten and antimony workings and a fully permitted processing facility. But the real prize here is vertical integration. Rather than simply digging critical minerals out of the ground and shipping concentrate elsewhere, American Tungsten is assembling the pieces to mine, process and produce higher-value antimony and tungsten products on US soil. That could prove particularly valuable as China tightens its grip on critical mineral supply chains. Both antimony and tungsten have seen ten-fold price increases over the previous five years and are some of the hottest commodities on the US governments radar for domestic production. Owning the mine, the refinery and the processing pathway domestically gives American Tungsten something most juniors can only dream about - a genuine mine-to-metal strategy inside the United States. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Clinical trial based on Richard Scolyer’s treatment offers new hope for brain cancer patients
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessBrain cancer Clinical trial based on Richard Scolyer’s treatment offers new hope for brain cancer patients Garry Maddox July 31, 2026 — 4:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is new hope for brain cancer patients with an Australian clinical trial based on Professor Richard Scolyer’s experimental treatment opening for newly diagnosed patients. Just weeks after the former Australian of the Year’s death, which came three years after he was diagnosed with a highly aggressive glioblastoma, the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne has confirmed the trial has started in this country. Professor Richard Scolyer’s experimental brain cancer treatment has led to a clinical trial which has opened in Australia. Alex Ellinghausen When it opened in the United States earlier this year, Scolyer said he was “incredibly excited” to see whether it could revolutionise the approach to treating glioblastoma. “It takes a long time to get trials over the line but to be actually recruiting patients in the United States – and hopefully here soon – means we can test out the drugs to see if they make a difference,” he said.



Related Article Vale ‘We treasure every moment’: Richard Scolyer’s children shine on a difficult, emotional day While he did not live long enough to see the opening of the Australian trial, there are hopes that the country’s pioneering approach to brain cancer will have benefits to patients around the world. Federal government data shows that more than 2000 Australians are diagnosed with brain cancer every year, accounting for just over 1 per cent of all cancer diagnoses. The five-year survival rate is just 24 per cent. The so-called GIANT trial will be for eligible patients with a new diagnosis of glioblastoma, based on an MRI scan, who are suitable for multiple surgical procedures as well as immunotherapy.



About 90 patients are expected to be recruited to the trial from around the world, with about half of them to be Australians from Peter Mac and Austin Health in Melbourne, and the Royal North Shore Hospital and Chris O’Brien Lifehouse in Sydney. Associate Professor Jim Whittle, an oncologist at Peter Mac and co-director of research strategy for the Brain Cancer Centre, said the study aimed to determine if the treatment was safe before it was expanded further. “This trial will explore the potential of a novel immunotherapy approach to improve outcomes for people with glioblastoma, a brain cancer for which there is a great need for new treatment options,” he said. “We are pleased to now open this trial to Australian patients.” Loading Because of the specific eligibility requirements, not all patients with a new diagnosis of glioblastoma would be eligible to participate.



Scolyer was diagnosed with an especially savage form of brain cancer – IDH wild-type glioblastoma – after a seizure on an overseas trip in mid-2023. Recognising that it was incurable, colleague and medical oncologist Professor Georgina Long proposed trying what she had learnt successfully treating advanced melanoma patients with immunotherapy. It was a risky plan that recognised that conventional treatment for brain cancer had barely changed in almost two decades. The treatment for the world-renowned pathologist and skin cancer researcher included receiving three immunotherapy drugs both before and after surgery to remove the bulk of the tumour, as well as radiotherapy and a personalised cancer vaccine. Scolyer and Long, who were co-medical directors of Melanoma Institute Australia, were jointly named 2024 Australian of the Year.



Related Article Obituaries Humble, heroic, selfless: Richard Scolyer beat the cancer odds but finally lost the battle While he was devastated when an operation revealed the tumour had returned in March last year, Scolyer survived more than twice as long as the median survival of 12 to 14 months. His death at the age of 59 was widely felt around the country, reflecting the humble and open way he had spoken about having cancer and the courage he had demonstrated in trying an experimental treatment that could have killed him quickly, in the hope of helping future brain cancer patients. Duke Cancer Institute in the US is the global lead for the GIANT trial. Australian medical oncologist Professor Mustafa Khasraw, an institute member from Duke University in North Carolina, said in February that he expected to know in about two years whether the treatment would be transformative.



He described the GIANT trial (for Glioblastoma Immunotherapy Advancement with Nivolumab and Relatlimab) as “team science” that was drawing together clinicians and scientists from many institutions around the world “to bring innovation and hope to patients”. Khasraw thought the trial was “absolutely a step in the right direction” for glioblastoma treatment. “It’s a stepping stone to generate convincing data that this therapy or a similar therapy is likely to improve patient outcomes at the population level,” he said. “We don’t want one patient to do better. We want all patients to do better.” A peer-reviewed paper on the treatment developed by Long, published in the international journal Nature Medicine last year, laid the groundwork for the trial. World.title: Silos lit up in pink as rural Victorian town farewells allegedly murdered 13-year-old girl
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Silos lit up in pink as rural Victorian town farewells allegedly murdered 13-year-old girl Lachlan Abbott July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Silos glowed pink and bubbles floated across a simple white coffin as the small country town of Donald gathered to remember a young life cut short. Hundreds of mourners from across the farming region in the state’s north-west attended Friday’s public memorial for 13-year-old Layla Jeffery, who was allegedly murdered by another child earlier this month. Donald teenager Layla Jeffery, whose body was one of four Australian women and girls allegedly murdered in four days in July. Police Media Bunches of pink balloons escorted Layla’s coffin outside before it was driven through a guard of honour in heart of the historic town of 1400 people. “Layla was a truly spectacular person who would have conquered the world if she hadn’t been taken from us,” said Layla’s aunt, Kaitlyn Cheyne, who delivered the eulogy.



Attendees at Layla’s memorial service were asked to wear a black hoodie or a Hello Kitty item to honour her. Layla’s father, Aaron, also read out a tribute. Her friends wrote messages on her coffin. An emotional compilation of photos was played. And, overnight, Donald’s grain silos were lit up in pink in Layla’s memory. The small community was rocked on Friday, July 10 when police searching for Layla announced they had discovered a body near the Richardson River the day before. Authorities had launched a major search after Layla was last seen on Saturday, July 4, and reported missing by a family member the next day. A 16-year-old boy from northern Victoria, who cannot be identified as he is a child, was charged with Layla’s murder on July 11.



Born in Shepparton in 2013, Layla spent time in Benalla and moved to Donald three years ago, her aunt said. “Though her years were far shorter than she deserved, over that time she grew into someone who felt a deep love for her family and friends, with a strong sense of self and the confidence to back it up,” Cheyne said. The silos in Donald were lit up in pink in honour of Layla Jeffery. Facebook “Though she was also something of a paradox because she often disliked being perceived, and liked to simply exist quietly alongside those she loved most.” Cheyne recalled the sounds of laughter when Layla had sleepovers with her friends, and fondly remembered her love of fashion, particularly jewellery and colouring her hair.



Layla always looked out for her friends and had a brilliant creative streak, Cheyne said. She loved her pets, music, movies like the Harry Potter series, and TV shows like Brooklyn Nine-Nine. “She was both shy and confident in many different ways – funny, sassy, kind, generous, stylish, sweet, cheeky, loving, and considerate,” her aunt said. Layla’s aunt, Kaitlyn Cheyne, speaks outside the family home earlier this month. Ashleigh McMillan “And I could go on and on and on, but it would still never be enough words to express the depth of her character or the loss we are all feeling.” The boy charged with Layla’s murder was due to face a children’s court on Friday, but his case was adjourned beforehand until late August.

World.title: ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced
World.content:
CultureArt & designVisual art ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced Elizabeth Flux July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Robert Fielding enters the room, he quietly takes in all the different artworks. His own is hung in one corner, but he walks straight up to another nearby – Minymaku Inma by Betty Campbell – then sits on the floor beneath it. He then makes his way across to Ngangkari Ngura (Healing Country) by Betty Muffler and does the same. Both artists, like Fielding, work in the APY Lands – and Campbell, like Fielding, works with Mimili Maku Arts. Hadley’s Art Prize 2026 winner Robert Fielding with his work Landscape. Jessica King Fielding’s work Landscape has been announced as the 2026 winner of the $100,000 Hadley’s Art Prize. He was first told the news over the phone, and now sitting in the gallery, his eyes start to fill with tears as recalls the moment he heard he had won. “I cried with tears of joy,” he says. “I had no words – and the two people came into my mind: my mum and my dad. Because when you see my artwork, it’s all about stolen generations.” It’s been a big year for the artist in an already soaring career. His portrait Tjintir-Tjintir was a finalist in this year’s Archibald, and Heritage impact assessment was a finalist in the Wynne prize.



Landscape is a scene that is mostly rendered in burnt red. Rundown cars are stacked on top of each other, tyres missing, doors open, windows gone. Down one side runs the word “Sacred”. Across the top reads “Nganampa” – ours. For Fielding, whose work also spans printmaking and photography, abandoned cars are a recurring motif, as vessels that house memory. “This is telling you a story of land … I’m very harsh with myself because when I paint, I paint for people,” he says. “I paint for movement. I paint for what was inside those relics. Who owned them? Who did they belong to?” he says. “They became heritage.” Run through Hobart’s Hadley’s Orient Hotel, the prize is one of the country’s richest for visual arts. This year, it was judged by Abdul Abdullah, Judith Ryan and Sarah Wallace. Works by Imants Tillers, Betty Muffler and Mia Boe. Jessica King



“It’s a very traditional mark-making process to tell a very contemporary and forward-looking story,” says Abdullah. “What drew me to it, even before we got into the room, was the way he wrote about it and his explanation.” Fielding’s work, Abdullah adds, “was interrogating landscape in a way that was unique in the prize”. Wallace says: “It’s a familiar sight that you see in a lot of places across Australia. But for him, it wasn’t something ugly or a blight on the landscape; it held memory and stories of Country, and travelling across Country.” The 26 finalist works on display at Hadley’s, in a pop-up downstairs gallery, offer a fascinating insight not only into the Australian landscape, but how it is perceived through different eyes. Walking through the exhibition, curator Dr Amy Jackett highlights details of each work. Bunuru Nocturne, Derbal yerrigan (High-Summer Night, Swan River) by Kelsey Ashe Jessica King



One of the few works on paper is watercolour and collage work Entanglement by Grace Gladdish. Emerald Coral by Ken Done is so vibrant it spills off the canvas and onto the frame. The winner of the prize’s residency award, Bunuru Nocturne, Derbal Yerrigan (High-Summer Night, Swan River) by Kelsey Ashe, is already unusual in that it depicts the landscape at night, then Jackett picks up a UV torch that makes the bioluminescent pigments glow wherever the light hits. Trill by Natasha Bieniek is so small and detailed it will be presented with a magnifying glass. The climate emergency is a recurring theme across the exhibition. Joe Blundell’s Tormented Land shows a scene of fallen trees, with the dirt between them littered with tracks of heavy machinery. It’s an idea that also drove Alice Mannheim’s work Log It!, which was awarded the Packing Room Prize. “I wanted to show that these environments are disappearing because people are destroying them through logging and deforestation,” Mannheim says. “I chose the Daintree rainforest because it’s very beautiful, but it’s also at risk of being destroyed.” Artist Alice Mannheim pictured with her work Log It! At 19, she is the prize’s youngest finalist, and this is the first time she has put her work forward for an award. She cites Harold Thornton’s portrait of Bob Brown, Dr Brown and Green Old Time Waltz, 1983, as an influence. She says that living in Canberra, “I’ve always been drawn to it.”



Her work is predominantly painted from memory, and she says: “I chose the title Log It! because it’s such a simple statement describing a simple action, but it has a very devastating impact.” The irony is deliberate – the beauty and detail of the rainforest versus the ease in which it can be eradicated. All the works – with the exception of Fielding’s, which has been acquired by Hadley’s – are for sale. “The prize to me means many things,” says Fielding. “It means many opportunities. I’m already planning.” For Fielding, this win is meaningful beyond a personal victory, and he emphasises the importance of paving the way for the next generation of artists and his work with Mimili Maku Arts in the APY Lands. “We’re here as a team, Mimili Maku Arts [to show] that art centres are our hub, our heartbeat, our unison, our grief, our sorrow, our finance, our fighting dream,” he says. “But most of all, it’s about respect.” The Hadley’s Art Prize exhibition is on at Hadley’s Orient Hotel, Hobart, from August 1-23.



Elizabeth Flux travelled to Hobart as a guest of Hadley’s Orient Hotel. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Bush trainer’s $5000 birthday gift ready to upstage $3m rival
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Bush trainer’s $5000 birthday gift ready to upstage $3m rival Craig Kerry July 31, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tony Ball saw plenty of expensive horse flesh during his decade-long stint as a foreman for Godolphin in Sydney, and he knows first hand that breeding and price tags can often mean little when it comes to how they perform on the racetrack. That’s partly why the Taree trainer has no qualms about taking $5000 buy Andrea to Rosehill for a first crack at Saturday city company, after he was balloted out of the Highway Handicap for country-trained horses. Andrea, right, tries to catch Sneaky Pee Cee in the Highway Handicap at Rosehill on July 18. Shannen Llewellyn rides him again on Saturday. Getty Images Coming off an eye-catching second in a Highway last start, Andrea will take on a field including Chris Waller-trained $3 million filly Ernaux, a daughter of I Am Invincible and Booker which has shown promise in city company but won only one race in 14 starts in the colours of American billionaire John Stewart. Ball has worked at both ends of the breeding and training spectrum. He enjoyed his time as a foreman under the leadership of Peter Snowden, John O’Shea and briefly James Cummings with Darley and Godolphin before later training his own team in the country.



“You see them come and you see them go, and everyone says they’ve got slow ones,” Ball said of the racing powerhouse. “Well, let me tell you, everyone’s got slow ones.” Trainer Tony Ball. Getty Images Ball now trains a team of 25 and he had 15 winners in the 2025-26 season, including a Canterbury victory with The Face. Xtra Approval gave him his other city winner in 2022 in a Rosehill Highway. He hopes Andrea can go a step higher to kick off the new season. The Graff gelding was held up briefly for a run last start before motoring home to almost catch Sneaky Pee Cee in a class 2 1100m Highway two weeks ago on heavy going. A $6 TAB chance, he steps up to 1200m on Saturday for a benchmark 72 handicap for three and four-year-olds.



“If you look at it, they are only class 3 horses, so it’s the same as the Highway,” Ball said. “And there’s only 10 in it now. He’ll go good and you never know. You can try him and just see how he goes. “If you’re not in it, you can’t win it, and he’s run third in a 64 in Sydney before. He’s consistent and he tries. He runs them down, he really finishes off. “There’s another Highway in a couple of weeks we might be able to get into. If he wins, we’ll just go day by day, that’s our attitude.” The bargain buy from the 2024 Inglis Classic Yearling Sale, owned by Ball’s wife, Barbara, and son, Michael, has two wins and four placings in 12 starts for a return of $75,338.



“I wish they were all like that,” Ball said. “My wife actually bought him for my son for his 40th birthday, and you are never going to believe why they bought him. “My wife loves Kitchwin Hill horses, and he had the KWH on him, and she saw him. “We’ve had quite a few of them and we’ve had luck with them, so we just keep picking one out occasionally and buy them. “We’ve got a stable full of young ones and you never know what’s around the corner for them.”



Related Article Horse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Rosehill on Saturday Scone stud Kitchwin Hills famously foaled and raised Melbourne Cup winner Vow And Declare and Everest champion Yes Yes Yes. Ball has fond memories of his time with Darley and Godolphin, which started out of the blue. “I was training in Queensland and my wife saw a job advertised and put in for it. I didn’t even know about it,” he said. “We got it, so we went down to Warwick Farm. We had a great time there and met some really nice people, and we’re still friends with them all down there. Brad Widdup was an assistant trainer and I worked under him, and I’m still great mates with him.”
